Introducing Vanna: An Open-Source Text-to-SQL Tool | Daily Dose of Data Science posted on the topic | LinkedIn
Finally! A Text-to-SQL tool that actually works!

(100% open-source, 20k+ stars)

Vanna is an open-source RAG framework for complex Text-to-SQL generation, designed for handling dynamic datasets. 

Works in 2 easy steps:

 1️⃣Train a RAG “model” on your data.
 2️⃣Ask questions in natural language which will return SQL queries that can be set up to automatically run on your database.

Key features:

 ✔High accuracy on complex datasets
 ✔Self-learning: improves with each query
 ✔ Secure: data never leaves your environment
 ✔Connect to any SQL DB (Snowflake, Redshift, etc.)
 ✔Multiple front-end integrations (Jupyter, Slack, etc.)

So, that probably tells you a little something about me.

I’m Kaitlyn, an owner and executive at NexGen, and posting about myself on LinkedIn is very far outside my comfort zone. I’d much rather be working behind the scenes than putting myself out in front.

One of the things I love most about working in the electric utility industry is that, behind all the projects, meetings, and day-to-day work, what we do has a very real purpose.

We help power communities and the future.

That's something I'm pretty proud to be a small part of.

29 days to go. Wish me luck.

A generic landing page does not automatically mean an AI slop website.

Yes, we’ve all seen the familiar patterns:
1. Big headline.
2. Purple gradient.
3. Bento-grid features.
4. “Revolutionize your workflow with AI.”

They can make a website feel generic but visual similarity alone tells us very little about the actual product.

A templated landing page can still lead to a useful, reliable product that solves a real problem. Meanwhile, a beautifully designed and completely original website can still hide broken features, fake testimonials, and little real value.

The better question is not:
“Does this website look AI-generated?”

It is:
“If we remove the polished visuals, does this product still provide meaningful value to a specific user?”

AI-assisted development is not the problem. The problem begins when generated output is treated as the finished product without enough judgment, testing, originality, or understanding of the user.

Generic design is a branding problem.

AI slop is a substance problem.

Store vs Warehouse vs Logistics: What Is the Difference?
Many people think Store, Warehouse, and Logistics mean the same thing, but they are completely different functions in the supply chain. Understanding these differences is essential for anyone working in inventory, warehouse operations, or logistics.

 📦 Store vs Warehouse vs Logistics – Do You Know the Difference?
Many people use these three terms interchangeably, but each has a unique role in the supply chain.
🔹 Store – Ensures materials are available for daily operations. Its focus is stock availability and issuing materials when needed.
🔹 Warehouse – Manages inventory efficiently through receiving, storage, picking, packing, and dispatch while maintaining high inventory accuracy.
🔹 Logistics – Connects the entire supply chain by transporting goods from suppliers to warehouses and finally to customers—on time and at the lowest possible cost.
From my 10+ years of experience in warehouse operations, I've learned that supply chain success doesn't depend on just one function. It depends on how well Store, Warehouse, and Logistics work together.
✅ Store keeps operations running.
✅ Warehouse keeps inventory under control.
✅ Logistics keeps business moving.
When these three functions are aligned, businesses achieve higher productivity, lower costs, and better customer satisfaction.

📊 Understanding the Balance Sheet: A Snapshot of a Company's Financial Health

One of the most important financial statements every finance student and professional should understand is the Balance Sheet.

A balance sheet provides a snapshot of what a company owns (Assets), owes (Liabilities), and the owner's share (Equity) at a specific point in time.

Here's a simple way to understand it:

✅ Assets – Resources owned by the company, such as cash, inventory, buildings, and equipment.

✅ Liabilities – Financial obligations the company needs to pay, such as loans, creditors, and outstanding expenses.

✅ Owner's Equity – The owner's investment in the business after deducting liabilities from assets.

The basic accounting equation is:

Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity

Why is a Balance Sheet important?

📌 It helps assess a company's financial position.
📌 It supports investment and lending decisions.
📌 It shows how efficiently a company manages its resources.
📌 It is one of the key financial statements used by managers, investors, and analysts.

As an MBA Finance graduate, I believe understanding financial statements is the foundation of making informed business decisions.

🚨 Common Resume Mistakes You Should Avoid

A strong resume does more than list your experience—it should quickly show employers why you're a great fit for the role. 📄✨

Here are 6 common mistakes that can reduce the impact of your resume:

❌ 1. Using a Generic Resume
🎯 Tailor your resume to the specific position and employer instead of sending the same version everywhere.

❌ 2. Writing a Weak Profile Summary
📝 Your opening summary should clearly communicate your experience, strengths, and career value.

❌ 3. Listing Responsibilities Without Achievements
🏆 Don't just say what you were responsible for. Highlight results, improvements, and measurable accomplishments.

❌ 4. Poor Formatting and Too Much Text
📋 Keep your resume clean, structured, and easy to scan. Recruiters often review resumes quickly.

❌ 5. Missing Job-Specific Keywords
🔑 Use relevant skills and keywords from the job description—especially important when resumes are screened by ATS systems.

❌ 6. Grammar, Spelling, and Formatting Errors
✅ Small mistakes can make a resume look careless. Always proofread before submitting.

💡 Remember: Your resume should be easy to read, relevant to the role, and focused on achievements—not just duties.

👉 Before applying for your next job, take a few minutes to review your resume against these six points.

Inversión extranjera directa: una inyección de confianza para la economía dominicana

La República Dominicana continúa consolidándose como uno de los destinos más atractivos para la inversión en América Latina y el Caribe. El crecimiento sostenido de la Inversión Extranjera Directa (IED) refleja algo más que la entrada de capitales: representa confianza en la estabilidad económica, el potencial productivo y las oportunidades de desarrollo que ofrece el país.

Detrás de cada inversión existen nuevas empresas, expansión de operaciones, generación de empleos, transferencia de conocimientos y oportunidades para fortalecer sectores estratégicos. Turismo, zonas francas, energía, tecnología, logística, manufactura y bienes raíces figuran entre las áreas que continúan captando el interés de inversionistas internacionales.

Este dinamismo también plantea importantes desafíos. El crecimiento de la inversión debe traducirse en mayor productividad, empleos de calidad, desarrollo regional y encadenamientos con las pequeñas y medianas empresas locales. La meta no debe limitarse a atraer más capital, sino a lograr que ese capital genere un impacto sostenible y ampliamente distribuido.

Para mantener esta trayectoria, será fundamental continuar fortaleciendo la seguridad jurídica, la transparencia institucional, la formación del talento humano y la infraestructura. Un entorno competitivo y predecible permite que la inversión no solo llegue, sino que permanezca, se expanda y contribuya al crecimiento de largo plazo.

La inversión extranjera directa es una señal clara de confianza, pero también una oportunidad estratégica. El reto para la República Dominicana consiste en convertir ese flujo de capital en innovación, competitividad y bienestar para más ciudadanos.

El crecimiento de la inversión es una buena noticia. Transformarla en desarrollo sostenible será la verdadera medida del éxito.

🎉 I have successfully completed my **8-week Generative AI Engineer Internship** with **Blackbucks Education Pvt. Ltd.** under **APSCHE**.

To everyone who is preparing for placements or working hard behind the scenes—keep going. Not every effort gets immediate recognition, but every effort shapes your future.

This is just the beginning. Many more milestones to achieve, many more lessons to learn, and many more stories to share.

Thank you to **Blackbucks Education Pvt. Ltd.**, **APSCHE**, my mentors, and everyone who has supported me throughout this journey.

It’s 10:47 p.m. on Day 1 of NexGen Utility Sales, LLC's 30-day LinkedIn challenge, and I’ve successfully avoided writing this post all day.

So, that probably tells you a little something about me.

I’m Kaitlyn, an owner and executive at NexGen, and posting about myself on LinkedIn is very far outside my comfort zone. I’d much rather be working behind the scenes than putting myself out in front.

But here’s the problem: I’ve surrounded myself with really smart people.

And those really smart people keep telling me that showing up here, sharing more about who we are, what we’re building at NexGen, and the lessons we’re learning along the way is good for our business. 

One of the things I believe most strongly about leadership is that you have to know your own strengths—and your weaknesses. You don't have to be the best person in the room at everything. In fact, you shouldn't be.

My strengths tend to live behind the scenes: strategy, legal, finance, compliance, risk mitigation, asking a lot of questions, and thinking several steps ahead. I also believe strongly in finding talented people, trusting them to do what they do best, and getting out of their way.

Apparently, tonight that means taking their advice and posting on LinkedIn. 😬  

So here I am. Day 1.

Over the next month, I’ll be sharing a little more about leadership, business, our team, and probably a few things that have absolutely nothing to do with what you’d expect from a polished executive.

And since I’m supposed to actually introduce myself today, I’ll end with this:

One of the things I love most about working in the electric utility industry is that, behind all the projects, meetings, and day-to-day work, what we do has a very real purpose.

We help power communities and the future.

That's something I'm pretty proud to be a small part of.

29 days to go. Wish me luck.

A generic landing page does not automatically mean an AI slop website.

Yes, we’ve all seen the familiar patterns:
1. Big headline.
2. Purple gradient.
3. Bento-grid features.
4. “Revolutionize your workflow with AI.”

They can make a website feel generic but visual similarity alone tells us very little about the actual product.

A templated landing page can still lead to a useful, reliable product that solves a real problem. Meanwhile, a beautifully designed and completely original website can still hide broken features, fake testimonials, and little real value.

The better question is not:
“Does this website look AI-generated?”

It is:
“If we remove the polished visuals, does this product still provide meaningful value to a specific user?”

AI-assisted development is not the problem. The problem begins when generated output is treated as the finished product without enough judgment, testing, originality, or understanding of the user.

Generic design is a branding problem.

AI slop is a substance problem.

Store vs Warehouse vs Logistics: What Is the Difference?
Many people think Store, Warehouse, and Logistics mean the same thing, but they are completely different functions in the supply chain. Understanding these differences is essential for anyone working in inventory, warehouse operations, or logistics.

 📦 Store vs Warehouse vs Logistics – Do You Know the Difference?
Many people use these three terms interchangeably, but each has a unique role in the supply chain.
🔹 Store – Ensures materials are available for daily operations. Its focus is stock availability and issuing materials when needed.
🔹 Warehouse – Manages inventory efficiently through receiving, storage, picking, packing, and dispatch while maintaining high inventory accuracy.
🔹 Logistics – Connects the entire supply chain by transporting goods from suppliers to warehouses and finally to customers—on time and at the lowest possible cost.
From my 10+ years of experience in warehouse operations, I've learned that supply chain success doesn't depend on just one function. It depends on how well Store, Warehouse, and Logistics work together.
✅ Store keeps operations running.
✅ Warehouse keeps inventory under control.
✅ Logistics keeps business moving.
When these three functions are aligned, businesses achieve higher productivity, lower costs, and better customer satisfaction.

📊 Understanding the Balance Sheet: A Snapshot of a Company's Financial Health

One of the most important financial statements every finance student and professional should understand is the Balance Sheet.

A balance sheet provides a snapshot of what a company owns (Assets), owes (Liabilities), and the owner's share (Equity) at a specific point in time.

Here's a simple way to understand it:

✅ Assets – Resources owned by the company, such as cash, inventory, buildings, and equipment.

✅ Liabilities – Financial obligations the company needs to pay, such as loans, creditors, and outstanding expenses.

✅ Owner's Equity – The owner's investment in the business after deducting liabilities from assets.

The basic accounting equation is:

Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity

Why is a Balance Sheet important?

📌 It helps assess a company's financial position.
📌 It supports investment and lending decisions.
📌 It shows how efficiently a company manages its resources.
📌 It is one of the key financial statements used by managers, investors, and analysts.

As an MBA Finance graduate, I believe understanding financial statements is the foundation of making informed business decisions.

🚨 Common Resume Mistakes You Should Avoid

A strong resume does more than list your experience—it should quickly show employers why you're a great fit for the role. 📄✨

Here are 6 common mistakes that can reduce the impact of your resume:

❌ 1. Using a Generic Resume
🎯 Tailor your resume to the specific position and employer instead of sending the same version everywhere.

❌ 2. Writing a Weak Profile Summary
📝 Your opening summary should clearly communicate your experience, strengths, and career value.

❌ 3. Listing Responsibilities Without Achievements
🏆 Don't just say what you were responsible for. Highlight results, improvements, and measurable accomplishments.

❌ 4. Poor Formatting and Too Much Text
📋 Keep your resume clean, structured, and easy to scan. Recruiters often review resumes quickly.

❌ 5. Missing Job-Specific Keywords
🔑 Use relevant skills and keywords from the job description—especially important when resumes are screened by ATS systems.

❌ 6. Grammar, Spelling, and Formatting Errors
✅ Small mistakes can make a resume look careless. Always proofread before submitting.

💡 Remember: Your resume should be easy to read, relevant to the role, and focused on achievements—not just duties.

👉 Before applying for your next job, take a few minutes to review your resume against these six points.

Inversión extranjera directa: una inyección de confianza para la economía dominicana

La República Dominicana continúa consolidándose como uno de los destinos más atractivos para la inversión en América Latina y el Caribe. El crecimiento sostenido de la Inversión Extranjera Directa (IED) refleja algo más que la entrada de capitales: representa confianza en la estabilidad económica, el potencial productivo y las oportunidades de desarrollo que ofrece el país.

Detrás de cada inversión existen nuevas empresas, expansión de operaciones, generación de empleos, transferencia de conocimientos y oportunidades para fortalecer sectores estratégicos. Turismo, zonas francas, energía, tecnología, logística, manufactura y bienes raíces figuran entre las áreas que continúan captando el interés de inversionistas internacionales.

Este dinamismo también plantea importantes desafíos. El crecimiento de la inversión debe traducirse en mayor productividad, empleos de calidad, desarrollo regional y encadenamientos con las pequeñas y medianas empresas locales. La meta no debe limitarse a atraer más capital, sino a lograr que ese capital genere un impacto sostenible y ampliamente distribuido.

Para mantener esta trayectoria, será fundamental continuar fortaleciendo la seguridad jurídica, la transparencia institucional, la formación del talento humano y la infraestructura. Un entorno competitivo y predecible permite que la inversión no solo llegue, sino que permanezca, se expanda y contribuya al crecimiento de largo plazo.

La inversión extranjera directa es una señal clara de confianza, pero también una oportunidad estratégica. El reto para la República Dominicana consiste en convertir ese flujo de capital en innovación, competitividad y bienestar para más ciudadanos.

El crecimiento de la inversión es una buena noticia. Transformarla en desarrollo sostenible será la verdadera medida del éxito.

AI時代のリーダーに求められるマインドセットは、好奇心・謙虚さ・判断力・信頼の4つ

小さく始め、早く学ぶ
AIを「人の代わり」ではなく「特定スキルを提供する仕組み」として設計する
業務プロセスを整えたうえでAIを乗せ、成功を称えながら文化として根づかせる

A small habit, an unexpected insight

Closing my eyes while listening is a habit I’ve had for a long time—even during Teams calls or meetings. My intention is simple: to focus more deeply on what the other person is saying.

Recently, I had an interesting experience that became an “aha” moment for me. During a Teams call, I did this as usual. After a moment, a person asked, “Are you okay?” She was concerned that I might not be feeling well or disengaged.

It surprised me.

This behavior, which feels natural—perhaps even culturally familiar from a Japanese perspective—was interpreted very differently in a global, remote setting. It reminded me of something important: In today’s environment, where we work across countries and cultures, it’s not always easy to understand how our actions are perceived. 

I took away two reflections from this: First, I need to be more mindful of how my behaviors might be interpreted by others—and avoid unintentionally creating confusion. Second, I truly appreciated that the person chose to ask directly. She didn’t make assumptions—she checked her understanding. That simple clarification prevented a potential misunderstanding.

To me, this is a great example of inclusive communication in action. Curious to hear your thoughts—have you had similar moments where intention and perception didn’t quite align?

Have a great weekend!

AI can now provide action lists—even for complex HR troubleshooting.

What used to be considered a “veterans-only” area, where years of experience mattered most, is increasingly supported by AI. During a recent session, I shared suggestions based on more than 30 years of HR experience. Interestingly, some participants immediately asked AI whether my points were correct. AI confirmed they were. 

That moment itself was symbolic. AI is very good at knowing and explaining. But HR—and leadership more broadly—is not just about knowing what to do. The hardest and most important part is taking responsibility and taking action.

AI cannot own decisions. AI cannot carry consequences. And without experience, knowing something does not automatically mean being able to do it. Learning how to do something is becoming easier than ever. The real core remains unchanged: to decide, to act, and to take responsibility as a human being.

That is where experience still matters—and where it always will.

A small cultural note that makes a big difference

In working with colleagues in Japan, one small detail can go a long way: the use of “-san.” Using “-san” isn’t just a linguistic habit — it’s a simple expression of respect, professionalism, and equality. While it’s perfectly fine to call someone by their first name without “-san,” using a last name without any honorific (for example, calling someone just “Yamada”) can come across as disrespectful.

From my own experience, being addressed by last name only usually happened in very specific contexts — school, among close friends, or in highly hierarchical environments. Even then, I personally avoided addressing others that way.

If someone calls me “Sugita (my last name)” without an honorific, I usually ask them to use “Kats (my first name)” or “Sugita‑san,” regardless of our relationship. Not because of formality — but because respect matters, and it’s often conveyed through small, thoughtful actions.

Being mindful of these nuances helps build trust and makes cross‑cultural collaboration smoother for everyone.

Unleashing Potential with Yoshuku: Visualizing Success Before It Happens

Like everyone else, I also have good days and bad days. Running is my best way to refresh my mind. During a run today, an idea suddenly came back to me: Yoshuku.

A few years ago, a professional Yoshuku practitioner was invited to our Tokyo headquarters, and around 30–40 people joined the session. I was one of them. At that time, I didn’t fully realize how deeply this concept connects with both our culture and modern business thinking. Yoshuku is a Japanese tradition of celebrating success in advance. Originally linked to prayers for a good harvest, it can be seen today as a form of success-oriented mental simulation. 

If we constantly imagine failure, our actions often follow that direction. But when we create concrete and detailed images of success, we begin to see what really matters—key actions, potential pitfalls, and risks we should avoid.

Inspired by this, I’ve decided to restart a personal Yoshuku routine every Monday—a moment to clearly and positively visualize success before it happens. I’m curious to see how this mindset will influence my thinking and actions over time, and I hope to share some good progress with you in the future.

Learning from Seno‑san: A Mindset for Growth

This week at our Tsukuba research site, we welcomed Teruo Seno, Japan’s most respected headhunter and executive coach. More than 60 colleagues joined, and the session was full of honest stories and lively conversations. 
One message from Seno‑san really stayed with me: Growth happens when we stay open to new experiences—not when we try to control a perfect career plan. He reminded us that the old “backcasting” style (deciding a future position and working backward) no longer fits a world that changes so quickly. Instead, he encouraged the “planned happenstance” mindset: Keep a broad direction, Stay curious, Say yes to opportunities that appear, And let new experiences shape the journey.
These days our organizations can change its direction or organizations so quickly. However, if we shift toward openness and learning, our careers don’t have to be limited by organizational changes. With a clear direction and a flexible mindset, each of us can continue growing, enjoying new challenges, and turning even surprises into opportunities.
I left Tsukuba inspired—and grateful.

As the new year dawns, and each breath of crisp morning air turns into a visible mist, many in Japan quietly make their way to a shrine. This tradition, marking the start of something new, is one of the beautiful aspects of Japanese culture. Despite the cold, after offering my prayers, I felt a gentle sense of clarity and refreshment, as if my mind had been reset for the year ahead.
 
In Japan, the traditional way of paying respect at a shrine—two bows, two claps, one bow—carries profound meaning. This ritual is more than a series of gestures:
• Bow twice: a moment to show respect and humility.
• Clap twice: a way to open your heart and express sincerity.
• Bow once again: a gesture of gratitude and closure.
This rhythm reminds me of the mindset we value in business: beginning with respect for others, showing sincerity through action, and ending with gratitude, which strengthens relationships and trust.
 
Perhaps you have your own rituals that bring clarity to your new year. I would love to hear how you greet the new year or what traditions inspire you as you set your goals for 2026.

Ekiden: A Lesson in Shared Purpose, Resilience—and Grace in Defeat

Every January, millions in Japan tune in to watch the Hakone Ekiden, a two-day, 217 km (135 mile) university relay race. It’s more than a sporting event—it’s a living example of leadership, teamwork, and character. The word Ekiden means “station to station,” rooted in an ancient courier system. Today, the sash (tasuki) symbolizes trust, responsibility, and continuity. Each runner pushes beyond personal limits, not for individual glory, but to honor the team and the shared goal. 

Sometimes, we witness something even more inspiring: grace in defeat.
I’ll never forget a team captain who gave a heartfelt speech after his team—expected to win after dominating two prior races—fell short. He thanked his general managers and teammates, made humble reflection of the race and then shouted, “I love my team!” despite the loss. Finally, he promised that his successors would win next year.
Moments like these remind us:
• We cannot always enjoy great business outcomes.
• Being a good loser—and learning from setbacks—is just as important as winning.
He embodied that spirit.

Ekiden is true teamwork:
• Success is a relay of effort, trust, and adaptability.
• Passing the baton—knowledge, responsibility, encouragement—is as critical as running your leg.
• Leadership means creating conditions where every runner feels their role is vital.

Every year, I cheer the runners in person. It’s my New Year ritual, and their determination gives me incredible energy. If you’re in Japan, I highly recommend experiencing it in person—or at least watching it on TV. You’ll gain a deeper understanding of Japanese culture and its emphasis on collective purpose: valuing the team over the individual, prioritizing endurance over speed, and cherishing the act of “passing on” responsibility. These principles are deeply woven into how Japanese organizations operate.

As we start a new year, let’s ask ourselves: “How can we design our teams to run like an Ekiden—aligned, resilient, and inspired by a common purpose?”

Great slides aren’t decoration—they’re strategy.

Too often we see the same deck used for a team update, an executive decision meeting, and a broad town hall. The result? Dense slides, tiny fonts, and audiences who can’t engage.

For me, slide design is both Inclusion and Business Effectiveness:
• Inclusion: Design for everyone in the room (and on the call). Use clear hierarchy, large readable fonts, high contrast, minimal jargon, and one message per slide. If people can’t read it, they can’t contribute.
• Plain Language for Global Audiences: Global leaders avoid overly sophisticated word choices because many listeners are non‑native English speakers. I appreciate that almost all Astellas senior leaders are mindful of this and consistently communicate so everyone can follow and contribute.
• Business Effectiveness: Tailor to the occasion. Executives need a crisp story and a clear “ask.” Broad communications need simplicity and clarity. Fewer, sharper slides improve decision velocity and alignment.

As leaders, our responsibility is to communicate accessibly and decide decisively. Let’s choose readability over density and clarity over completeness—and get better outcomes for our people and our business.

What’s one change you’ll make to your slide design or language in your next meeting? Share a tip (or an example) in the comments—and tag a colleague who does this well.

Inclusion at Astellas: business discipline that creates VALUE for patients
Inclusion at Astellas isn’t a slogan—it’s the way we turn innovative science into real‑world outcomes for patients. When we all stay relentlessly business‑oriented, inclusion becomes practical and measurable: we learn what the business needs, and we co‑create solutions that move the business.
To keep that discipline, our meetings run on a one‑page proposal. On a single page we capture:
• Topic
• Why now (why this deserves the meeting)
• Options (viable solutions)
• Today’s recommendation & why
• Timeline
• Cost proposal
Charts or a table can be attached, but only the one‑pager is presented on the day—because clarity invites diverse voices, focuses debate on decisions, and accelerates execution. At Astellas, if a proposal is not presented as a one‑pager, it will not be tabled for discussion or approval.
Inclusion is also imagination. It asks: What do they need? How can I support them? Without imagination, we cannot work well in any organization. Imagination helps us anticipate needs, design better options, and include perspectives that might otherwise be missed.
From my experience as CPO at Astellas, initiatives go well when we follow this guideline. When we don’t, even high‑quality proposals face challenges. The difference is business‑side buy‑in and understanding the audience—without those, HR initiatives risk becoming self‑satisfaction rather than business impact.
HR experts often default to technical explanations, but what the business truly needs is a clear line of sight to how the proposal drives our business—pipeline impact, operational efficiency, and patient outcomes. HR is part of the business, not adjacent to it. Thinking from that point of view is critical.
When we combine diverse perspectives with business rigor, we make faster, smarter decisions—and that’s how we win for patients and for Astellas.

Before having a dog, my weekend time management was more relaxed. But now, with this routine, I can get a lot done in the mornings on Saturdays and Sundays. I can go for a long-distance run, catch up on reading, and spend quality time with my wife discussing various topics. This sense of accomplishment and the extra energy it brings is quite rewarding.
Engaging in active recovery not only refreshes me but also promotes better balance. Exercise allows my brain to take a break and my muscles to release tension, leading to a more refreshed and balanced state. I hope you find this concept as beneficial as I do. Have a great day ahead!

I recently came across a message that resonated with me, and I wanted to share it with all of you as I believe it could significantly enhance our workflow and communication. The message stated: "If I do not receive any response from you prior to [specified deadline], I will assume you have no edits to this latest draft, and I will proceed."
 
I think this approach is fantastic for maintaining a sense of urgency and ensuring that projects move forward without unnecessary delays. It is both polite and effective, and it fosters accountability. By not responding, you are essentially signaling trust and delegation, which can be very empowering.
 
Many years ago, I had the experience of working with a great supervisor who was in a different country. Despite their many strengths, their response speed was a weak point that often slowed down my work. This situation led to frustration and a realization that I needed a better way to manage communication. My mentor recommended the same proactive communication technique “if I don’t receive…”, and it dramatically changed my professional life.
 
By using this approach, I was able to control my work and plan my timing more effectively. It required me to be outcome-focused and accountable for the results, but it also provided a sense of empowerment and control over my schedule. I highly recommend this method to all of you. It allows you to plan your actions and manage your timing independently, leading to improved efficiency and productivity. It will increase your white space, definitely.

Integrity Comes First, In Every Decision We Make

Earlier this year, we launched our Organizational Values & Behaviors, with Integrity intentionally placed first.

For me, this is more than symbolic as everything we do starts with doing the right thing. It’s the foundation of trust, and the basis for how we work together as One Astellas. Two recent milestones show how we are putting this into action.

The first is the launch of our updated Code of Conduct. Originally introduced in 2016, it has now been completely redesigned to be clearer, more practical, and more relevant to the realities of our work today. It’s a guide to help all of us make sound decisions, collaborate across borders, and speak up when something doesn’t feel right. I’m proud that over 100 colleagues contributed to shaping the new Code, which makes it something we all own together.

The second is the success of our Ethical Leadership workshops, delivered jointly by Ethics & Compliance and HR. 500 senior leaders and managers from every region have already participated and the feedback has been very encouraging. Every single participant said the workshop deepened their understanding of the role leaders play in modelling Integrity, and almost all said they feel more confident building trust and transparency in their teams.

For me, Integrity is not a policy, it’s a daily practice. It’s how we lead when no one is watching, how we support each other, and how we build a culture where everyone feels safe to speak up and do the right thing. It’s no mistake this is the first of our three Values: Integrity; Innovation and Impact.

As leaders, it starts with us. The Code and the workshops are important tools, but what matters most is the consistency of our actions, big and small, every day.

Let’s Break the Silence Around Menopause at Work

For too long, menopause has been treated as a private issue, when it is clearly a workplace one too. Our global Menopause Experience and Attitudes Study, covering 13,800 respondents across six countries, shows just how widespread the impact is:
- Over a third of people going through menopause experience some kind of negative impact at work.
- 1 in 20 believe they’ve lost out on promotions or pay rises.
- Many feel unable to talk to colleagues or managers.

This is a reality we can and must change.

That’s why I’m proud to support Astellas’ Pledge to Champion a Menopause-Inclusive Workplace. Through education, training, and open dialogue, we aim to create a culture where no one feels they have to suffer in silence.

This is about health, inclusion, and respect.

It’s also a reminder that leadership means listening, even when the topic is uncomfortable. It is especially important we listen then.

A recent conversation with people from the media gave me a chance to reflect on the evolving role of HR and the essence of human capital management.

Why do we need an HR department in the first place? My time at a global company challenged my assumptions more than any other experience. Before joining, I led HR for a Japanese subsidiary, where I naturally took the lead in talent and organizational discussions during regional and HQ reviews. It felt like a clear part of HR’s job. But at the company, the expectation was different. HR’s role was to coach and prepare business leaders—both regional / HQ and local—so they could lead meaningful conversations about talent and organization themselves.　At first, I thought, “It would be faster and more effective if I just did it myself.” But I soon realized: this is the point.

Talent and organizational matters are as fundamental to business as finance. As global leaders often say, “Finance in one hand, HR in the other.” Strong leaders take ownership of hiring, development, rewards, and culture. They don’t delegate these decisions and accountabilities entirely to HR—they shape them as part of their business strategy.

It may take more effort upfront, but unless business leaders truly own their talent and organizational challenges, HR initiatives risk being seen as disconnected or “just another program.” This isn’t about HR simply following business. It’s about HR identifying challenges, proposing solutions, and guiding leaders until they feel the challenge is their own.

I’d love to hear your thoughts. How is HR evolving in your organization?

I recently came across some fantastic insights on the importance of asking questions, particularly from Michael Marquardt and Bob Tiede's work – Leading with Questions. It reminded me of a tech giant CEO who always encouraged employees to ask questions, demonstrating an incredibly strong growth mindset. This practice has made me realize that asking questions is a key behavior that I often forget. I tend to jump straight to answers or recommendations, which isn't always the best approach.

Many exceptional leaders talk less and ask more questions, guiding their teams in the right direction. Even asking seemingly "stupid" questions can be beneficial, as it fosters a sense of psychological safety within the team. When leaders ask questions, it shows that it's okay for others to do the same. This approach is particularly useful when dealing with topics we're not entirely familiar with, as it allows us to delegate tasks more effectively.

It's essential to remember that asking questions shouldn't come across as accusatory. Instead, it requires good listening skills and can help resolve conflicts. Confident leaders aren't afraid to ask questions, as they understand that it doesn't make them appear weak. Some valuable questions to ask include: "How can I help you?", "What do you need to make it even better or quicker?", "What could we have done better?", "What would you do if you had the chance again?", "If we don't do this, what will happen?", and "What can be the best and worst-case scenarios?".

Ultimately, everything ties back to having a growth mindset for the future. I'm eager to continue improving my questioning skills and would love to hear your thoughts on this topic.

With AI, the distance between “I have an idea” and “I have something real” has never been smaller.

I recently spoke at Workhuman Live in Orlando about the fear and anxiety so many people are feeling right now. I asked the room to consider the parent who stepped away from the workforce to raise their kids — managing schedules, navigating crises, coming up with solutions on the fly, and maybe carrying a business idea in the back of their mind the whole time.

AI can help them go from concept to a first draft, a business plan, a website outline, a customer email, without needing to know all the technical steps up front. That’s a big deal, because it can turn the idea they have into momentum.

This is why I challenged my fellow HR leaders to step into this moment.
The fear is real. But so is what’s on the other side of it:

The future where the parent says, “I didn’t know I could do that,” right before they become a builder.

The future where the employee who saw AI as a threat discovers it’s the thing that finally frees them to do their best work.

That’s the future we get to build, together.

One of the most important things I do as CPO is listen. Listen to what's on people's minds, what's keeping them up at night, what they wish we'd do more (or less) of.

We can’t ask people to work in new ways, and then measure, reward, and manage them like nothing has changed. 
 
The 2026 Microsoft Work Trend Index puts data behind a conversation I’m hearing everywhere, something we’re calling the Transformation Paradox. 
 
People feel real urgency to move fast with AI.  
Yet many still default to what feels safe. 
And very few feel rewarded for actually reinventing how they work. 
 
We found that factors like culture, manager support, and talent practices drive more than 2x the impact of individual mindset and behavior. So how do we unlock that impact? 

• Model it: Use AI visibly. Share how it’s reshaping your day, what it’s unlocking in your own work. 
• Make it relevant: Changing the way we work can’t feel like a one-time sprint. Connect it directly to your team’s priorities 
• Reinforce it: Build and reward new habits and new ways of working until they become the default on your team. 

If we want different outcomes, we have to create different conditions for how work gets done.

Yesterday marked my first anniversary as Microsoft's Chief People Officer. There’s no question in my mind that this is the company I want to be at — and the team I want to be on — as the world continues to change. 
 
The world of work is complex, exciting, and moving at a pace I’ve never seen before. And yet, the principle guiding our decisions every day is simple: if what we’re doing isn’t accelerating the business and helping teams do their best work, we should pause and ask why we’re doing it at all. 
 
Here’s what I know to be true as I step into year two: 
 
Clarity beats complexity. Talking to each other like humans in simple, plain language unlocks speed, understanding, and trust. 
 
Build with, not just for. Pressure‑test assumptions and stay customer‑obsessed, especially when the customer is our employees. Now more than ever, we have to stay close to the business, pay attention to what’s working (and what isn’t), and adjust quickly.  
 
Unlearning matters just as much as learning. Too often, holding onto what once worked slows down progress. When we’re willing to let go of what was, we expand what’s possible. We create space for better ideas, faster decisions, and stronger outcomes. 
 
To every person I've had the chance to connect with this year — our employees across the globe, my peers, our customers — thank you. You are the reason this work is worth doing and I’m honored to work alongside you. Here's to year two!

Some of the most inspiring women in my life are just getting started. Others are choosing to become beginners again—embracing a mid‑career pivot into something new. 

As I reflect on #WomensHistoryMonth, I’m grateful for the many women who inspire me personally and professionally.  

At the very top of that list are my three girls. I’m in awe of how they are navigating college, internships, and early career decisions with grace, adaptability, and deep intellectual curiosity. One thing they’ve all done is left home to go to college, thousands of miles away.  

As a parent, I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about what I can do to help prepare them for the workforce. As a CPO, I’m acutely aware that the workplace they’re entering looks completely different than the one I stepped into. 
 
And yet, I often find they’re already demonstrating the qualities that matter most right now: 
Adaptability – In times of rapid change, the ability to reassess, pivot, and keep moving forward, even without perfect information. 
Humility – Being curious, admitting what you don’t know, and staying open to learning something new. 
Courage – Taking the first step into any career moment (whether it’s your first or your thirty‑first) requires turning fear into fuel and backing yourself.

Rahul Jindal's latest paper on “Organizational Metabolism” is a masterclass in shifting our focus from AI adoption to AI absorption. His core thesis? The real differentiator in 2026 isn't your technology budget—it’s your "Metabolic Rate."
The framework’s biggest win is the concept of Workflow Debt. We are often layering AI on top of legacy processes instead of retiring them. As Rahul puts it: "Low-metabolism organizations accumulate experiments. High-metabolism organizations retire workflows."
The one piece I think we still need to solve for: The Emotional Metabolism.
While the structural roadmap is brilliant, we can’t ignore the "human immune system." Retiring a workflow can feel like retiring an identity. For an organization to truly become "Adaptive," we have to figure out how to build the psychological safety that allows teams to dismantle their own processes without fearing for their future.

The agentic enterprise is here! 🚀

Yesterday, I had the honor of moderating an incredibly inspiring World Economic Forum session on AI and the future of work, with two visionary leaders Judson Althoff and Carl Eschenbach. Yesterday’s discussion made it clear that while AI continues to transform our world, it is our people – with their creativity, adaptability, and judgment – who are powering the future. 

We came away with three clear lessons leaders can use when empowering people to lead with AI:

1. Optimism over anxiety. The conversation is shifting, and employees are increasingly hopeful about what AI can do for them and their organizations. Success starts with leaders who champion and empower their teams to see challenges as opportunities. 

2. AI is for everyone. Universal adoption is key. AI should amplify every employee’s impact, regardless of their role. Commit to championing AI literacy in your organization, ensuring every person has the confidence and skills to thrive alongside AI tools. 

3. AI is the tool, but people are the power. Your people are the engine of transformation – fuel them. As leaders, we must invest in both cutting-edge tools and world-class training equally. When we do both, we do more than adopt AI – we lead the future.

🔹 At Walmart the future of work will be people-led and tech-powered. Jobs will evolve, new roles will emerge and definitely there will be work and jobs that change. Our responsibility is to help equip people with the skills and support to grow through that change.

🔹 Career pathways matter. As technology changes how work gets done, companies have an opportunity to choose to create pathways for associates to build new skills and move into growing roles.

What stays with me in moments like this isn’t the policy change. It’s the people behind it.
 
In too many rural communities, health care can feel stretched thin with limited resources, complex processes and real pressure on the people delivering care.
 
Care teams are often small, but deeply rooted in the places they serve. They’re not just providers — they’re neighbors, lifelines and a source of stability when everything else feels far away.
 
That’s why reducing administrative burden and speeding up payments matters. It’s giving time back to a nurse covering two roles. It’s helping a physician focus on a patient instead of paperwork. Because supporting the people who deliver care is how we make health care work better. Especially in the places that need it most.

Raise your hand, opportunities are what you make them!

Today is National Intern Day. And right now, there are hundreds of incredibly bright and energetic young people wrapping up their summer at UnitedHealth Group. Drawn to our mission – to help people live healthier lives and help the health system work better for everyone – they’re gaining skills and experiences they’ll carry with them as they set out to do good in the world, here and beyond. 

My journey to health care started with an internship, too. I was fortunate to get a foot in the door of a Boston hospital. That summer, I was one of two interns working in the department. I was an undergrad. The other person was working on her master’s – and more than happy to brush all the grunt work my way. As it happens, she also helped me learn a most valuable lesson: Opportunities are what you make them.

One morning, our manager let us know there was a big meeting coming up. He asked if we could help. I raised my hand (she didn’t) and volunteered to stay late to put the briefing packets together, thinking maybe…just maybe...they’d let me come to the meeting. And they did. 

The next day, I showed up early in my red suit – my only suit – and found a seat. As the meeting got underway, one of our guests, the powerful Speaker of House for Massachusetts wrapped up his talk and asked if there were any questions. I took a deep breath, raised my hand and asked my question. Apparently, I made an impression. Because months later, he called the hospital. He was looking for someone to help him put together some focus groups and asked our boss, “what about that lady in the red suit?”
 
The rest of my career unfolded from there. 

If I hadn’t been willing to skip happy hour and stand at the copy machine working the three-hole punch, I might never have met a mentor who helped open a door to HR, which led to another door into law school, which led to a door to technology, and then another back to health care. 

So, as the summer intern season comes to a close, I want to extend my deepest appreciation to our incredible interns – for showing up with such great energy, perspective and a genuine eagerness to learn. It’s been truly inspiring to watch you grow. Keep showing up, keep raising your hands and keep building your networks, because you never know what opportunity will come your way. And remember this advice my mentor shared with me: “Be seen. Be heard. Be memorable.”

A few days after Valentine’s Day, I was reminded that “heart” isn’t just a symbol for love but for life. ❤️🧡

I was grateful to join the Heart-to-Heart event organized by our LEAD (Leading Employees of African Descent) employee resource group in observance of Black History Month and American Heart Month, raising awareness of chronic heart health within the Black community.

According to the American Heart Association, cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death for African Americans, with nearly 60% of Black adults (aged 20+) living with some form of CVD. During the session, our medical director Dr. Cara Pensabene, MD shared that prevention and management of cardiovascular disease start with awareness and access. Wellness benefits, like what we offer at Mastercard, support the mind, body, financial, and social well-being of our people. These are not “nice to have”; they reflect how we empower our employees to thrive, embracing flexibility and anchoring our culture in purpose and growth opportunities.

One key takeaway for me was this: even with full calendars, we have to be intentional about making time for self-care and focusing on what truly makes a difference. For me, that means moving more. I encourage you to prioritize your health and help spread awareness too.

#BlackHistoryMonth #AmericanHeartMonth #Wellbeing #WeAreMastercard

I recently read an article titled "Want to Get the Most Out of AI? Put People First" — a timely reminder that the success of AI adoption depends less on technology and more on how we bring our people along.

At Mastercard, we’re focused on bridging that gap — creating open dialogue about how AI impacts work, while investing in learning and reskilling for our people. 

That was a key theme at this week’s People & Capabilities Town Hall, where we explored how AI is reshaping the future of work — not just through new tools, but through new ways of thinking. AI is changing how we work, but it’s our people who will shape what that future looks like.

I've been thinking...about context.
  
As AI becomes increasingly capable of delivering information, I've found myself reflecting on one leadership skill I believe is becoming even more valuable to every organization's success: providing context.
  
Information has never been more accessible. Context has never been more important.
  
Context lives in the space between the data and the decision. It's understanding the history behind an issue before determining the next step, recognizing when a team's reaction is influenced more by previous experiences than the current situation, hearing what isn't being said in a meeting, and knowing when to ask one more question.
  
Recently, my team was reviewing a data trend that seemed to tell a very clear story. Without context, we could have over-indexed on the wrong solution and distracted our businesses from delivering the life-changing work our customers depend on.
  
Once we layered in organizational history and understood what had changed, the data told a very different story.
  
The numbers hadn't changed – our understanding had. That's the power of context.
  
AI will continue to get better at generating information. It will summarize, analyze, and identify patterns faster than ever before. But context still requires experience, judgment, curiosity and an understanding of people.
  
In a world where information is becoming abundant, context may become a leader's greatest contribution – perhaps one of the most uniquely human forms of leadership.
  
What do you think will become more – not less – uniquely human about leadership in the age of AI?

In a recent conversation with one of our Business Resource Groups, I was asked about strategies for moving into #leadership roles and it made me reflect on the important distinction between being managed and being mentored.

Both are essential – managers help us succeed where we are, mentors help us prepare for what’s next.

Great managers build performance. They set clear goals, coach through challenges, hold people accountable and remove barriers to team success. 

Great mentors build perspective. They help you zoom out – think strategically about your growth, test ideas, and explore what’s next. A strong mentor challenges your assumptions and helps you see possibilities you might not see yourself. 

If you are aspiring to lead, or even just accelerate your own development, here’s where you can start:

– Find a mentor who checks the right boxes.
 □ Has the skills, judgment or influence you want to build
 □ Is known for developing others and consistently leading high-performing teams
 □ Will offer honest feedback, including the tough truths to push and support you
 □ Sits outside your reporting line to allow more freedom for curiosity and candid exploration

– Use the time with your mentor to discuss lessons learned from their experiences, both successes and setbacks, as well as what you’re currently experiencing. 

– Engage your manager in open conversation about your goals and how to create stretch opportunities.

– Pair your mentor’s perspective with your manager’s coaching for greatest impact.

And if you already lead, be both – a strong manager who develops people today, and a mentor who invests in the leaders of tomorrow. Results always matter, but the greatest legacy is leaving behind those truly ready to lead.

#GrowthMindset #LifeatThermoFisher

– Put the Wrench Down: Why ROI Starts with People – 
  
There’s a fine line between what we can do and what we should do. I learned that the hard way—not in the office, but under my kitchen sink on a Saturday morning.

With a wrench in hand and YouTube at my side, I was determined to fix a stubborn hot water valve. But I realized something: sure, I could try. But at what cost? A flooded kitchen? Hours wasted? Instead, I called a plumber.

That small moment reminded me of something far bigger—the curse of competence. Just because we’re capable doesn’t mean it’s the best use of our time, energy or expertise.

In #HR, this shows up everywhere. We tell ourselves, “It’s easier if I just do it myself.” 

But real impact comes when we invest in the right skills, empower others and align work where it belongs—whether that’s business partners driving outcomes, specialized experts elevating the function or colleague self-service.

Over my 30+ years in HR, I’ve seen our profession transform from administrators to business enablers. The greatest #ROI isn’t in doing everything ourselves—it’s in unlocking the potential of people and maximizing efficiency.

Sometimes the smartest move is to put the wrench down. Because when we stop trying to do it all, we create space for growth, innovation and real returns—on skills, on people and on business results.

#strategicHR #HReffectiveness

September always feels like a reset – a reminder that none of us are ever too senior, too experienced or too established to keep learning. One of the most powerful, and sometimes overlooked, ways to grow is through #apprenticeship. 

At Thermo Fisher Scientific, we view apprenticeship as more than mentoring. It’s a two-way exchange between expert and learner, where both are developing, not just delivering. It’s a mutual investment built on trust, feedback and real-time collaboration.

—  For the expert, apprenticeship means sharing your thought process, creating scaffolds that empower independence, and coaching through real challenges – knowing when to step back so others can step up.
—  For the apprentice, it’s about watching closely, asking questions, articulating your reasoning and taking ownership of your growth. Over time, that practice builds both confidence and capability.

When done well, apprenticeship doesn’t just shape individuals – it builds a culture where learning is continuous, feedback is natural and teaching is everyone’s responsibility. That’s the kind of culture I want to be part of.

Looking back, I’ve been fortunate to experience both sides. I’ve learned the mechanics of a balance sheet from a former CFO and the basics of plumbing from my dad. Both shaped how I think, work and lead. And in turn, being able to teach others those same lessons has been one of the most rewarding experiences of my career – and my life.

As this new season begins, I invite you to reflect: What are you learning? Who are you teaching? And how can we each show up as both expert and apprentice?

Here’s to learning, always – together.

A new IBM Institute for Business Value global study highlights a growing disconnect many business leaders are seeing. Nearly two-thirds of executives say AI is reshaping roles and workflows yet most organizations have not redesigned the people systems needed to support that shift. 
 
The result? A widening gap between how leaders report AI progress and how employees actually experience it. 
 
A few findings stood out: 
➡️ Permission: 70% cite unclear authority is causing issues in AI projects. 
➡️ Practice: 93% say AI-enabled work is harder to evaluate. 
➡️ Proof: 81% of executives believe employees are rewarded for AI skills, but only 64% reward employees who challenge AI outputs. 

The takeaway isn’t that AI strategies are failing. It’s that organizational change hasn’t kept pace with technological change. 
 
The organizations that succeed won’t simply deploy AI faster. They’ll help employees understand how work is changing, what skills are becoming more valuable and where new opportunities are emerging. More importantly, they’ll make employees active participants in shaping the future of work. Because the people best positioned to redesign work are often the ones doing it every day.

One of the biggest mistakes in HR transformation isn’t choosing the wrong AI model or platform.
 
It’s conceptual failure.
 
Many leaders in HR (and other disciplines, honestly) still think of AI as a distinct program or initiative. But AI isn't a program – it’s a permanent shift in how work gets done. That means cascading changes to everything from talent, to skills, to (entry-level) hiring.
 
I wrote about this for Fortune, below. #AI #HR #Transformation
 
P.S. You often hear that AI will automate rote tasks and unlock “higher-value work.” How do you define that higher-value work?

Thank you, Chip Cutter, for the conversation about HR and AI last week. (And congratulations to WSJ Leadership Institute on the inaugural CPO Council Summit!)
 
CPOs and CHROs are under intense pressure to undergo AI transformation. But what does success look like? We discussed how:
 
1. AI-powered productivity is the means, not the end. Growth is the end goal. Couple that extra time with talent for true results. This is why IBM is tripling entry-level hiring.
 
2. Value can be measured in (many) more ways than one, from time saved to downstream growth. On the flip side, remember: AI usage isn't free. Every query comes with a cost. 
 
3. No matter how sophisticated the technology becomes, HR leaders always need to prioritize the employee experience. Tech *in service of* the experience.
 
4. Please, please, please: Don't put agents on org charts. Especially if that technology isn't actually an agent.

What does AI mean for your talent strategy? How do you prepare for it?

Huge thanks to Paulo Carvao, former IBMer and Senior Fellow at Harvard University, for this great article in Forbes about how AI is redefining the future of work.

Here are my top three insights:

1️⃣ Economic growth through human-AI collaboration
AI delivers its greatest value when it augments, not replaces, human capabilities. Organizations that design work to combine human judgment with AI efficiency will see productivity gains that help fuel long-term growth.

2️⃣ Skills are the new competitive advantage
The rate and pace of technological change demand continuous learning. Both employees and employers alike must do their part to invest in the skills development necessary for future success.

3️⃣ Productivity with purpose
AI can automate tasks, but the real opportunity lies in freeing up employees to focus on the more strategic work that involves creativity, innovation and problem-solving, which drives differentiation and engagement.

How are you rethinking skills development and redesigning work in the AI Era? I’d love to hear your perspective. #AI #GenAI #skills

Last week, we hosted a global broadcast at Pfizer on becoming an AI-fluent organization. The session came on the heels of launching our “AI Foundational Essentials” course to every colleague across the company, an important step in building the skills needed to thrive in an AI-powered future.

We were joined by two leading researchers, Kate Niederhoffer & Jeff Hancock, who study how AI is reshaping the way we work. Their message was clear: tools and training matter, but they are only the hard wiring. Successful AI adoption highly depends on the soft wiring, or the mindset, we bring.

Kate and Jeff described the difference between Pilots and Passengers. Pilots approach AI with curiosity, optimism, and a sense of agency, using it as a tool to challenge their thinking and explore different perspectives. The research shows these are the individuals most likely to unlock new ideas, accelerate execution, and help organizations realize the potential of AI.

Passengers, on the contrary, tend to hand tasks over to AI and let it do the thinking for them. While that can improve efficiency, it often misses the critical opportunities for reflection and creativity that drive innovation. 
 
Building a Pilot mindset across the organization is as much about how we work together as it is about the tools we put in people's hands. As Kate and Jeff put it, "AI is not a single-player game." 
 
For organizations striving to become AI-fluent, the goal is not simply greater adoption, it’s creating more Pilots.

Thank you to Kate, Jeff, Albert Bourla and BetterUp for a fantastic conversation, and to our colleagues who continue to embrace this evolution with openness and curiosity.

This week, we hosted a global broadcast at Pfizer for Mental Health Awareness Month, and I was honored to be joined by the incredible Arianna Huffington for a conversation on all things mental health. We covered topics like the science of sleep, brain health, the power of physical connection, and how AI can help us reconnect with what makes us human.

Here are my top takeaways:

▪️ Stress is inevitable, but cumulative stress is avoidable. In as little as 60 seconds of conscious breathing, or focusing on something that brings you joy, you can interrupt the stress cycle. Small, consistent micro-steps will outlast big, unsustainable resolutions.
▪️ You can't pour from an empty cup. Whether you're a caregiver, a leader, or both, taking care of yourself isn't selfish — it's how you show up fully for the people who need you.
▪️ As AI becomes more capable, being human becomes more valuable. Resilience, empathy, creativity, and connection aren't soft skills anymore. They're the skills that matter most when intelligence alone is no longer a differentiator.

Thank you, Arianna, for a conversation that was both grounded in science and full of heart - you never fail to leave us with a renewed sense of optimism. And thank you to everyone who tuned in! 

#MentalHealthAwarenessMonth

Some of the most powerful innovations don’t start in a lab - they start in communities.

Years ago, Medtronic teams partnered locally in Ghana to help build a care platform designed around real community needs. It pairs community health workers with patients and uses an AI-enabled platform to monitor and guide care.

This is what happens when we listen first and design with humility - solutions scale while staying rooted in what matters most.

The most productive thing you can do today? Embrace JOMO. We’ve all been raised on FOMO (Fear Of Missing Out), but in the corporate world, FOMO is just a polite term for a bottleneck.

If you feel the need to be in every 30-person meeting to "stay aligned," you aren't leading; you’re hovering. If you need to be CC'd on every email thread to "feel informed," you aren't empowering; you’re slowing the engine.

At Verizon, we are architecting an AI-enabled ecosystem to eliminate "the mundane". But tech alone won't give us speed. We need a cultural pivot from "Agreeable to Accountable".

JOMO - The Joy of Missing Out —is the ultimate leadership flex. * It’s the joy of trusting your team to take "Total Ownership" of the talent lifecycle without you in the room.

When we stop trying to be everywhere, we finally give our leaders the space to be innovative and quick. Speed doesn't come from more eyes on a project; it comes from fewer, more decisive ones.

Let’s stop rewarding "presence" and start rewarding "impact."
Who’s brave enough to decline that 4:00 PM "update" meeting and trust the team to handle it? That’s the BOLD standard.

Checking in with ourselves shouldn’t feel like a rare act of care. It should be part of how we work, lead and live. Because emotional resilience starts with awareness — noticing when we’re stretched thin, speaking up when we need help, and making it safe for others to do the same.

If you lead a team, make check-ins part of your rhythm and rituals. Ask how people really are — and be ready to listen. Create the space, model the behaviors and show that care isn’t a policy — it’s an essential practice.

When we care for ourselves and each other, we build stronger teams, deepen trust and deliver better results. Because people who feel seen and supported bring their best — to work and to life.

So let’s make “How are you doing?” more than a greeting. Let’s make it a habit.

Some of the best career advice I’ve ever received had nothing to do with strategy, skill-building or networking. It was this:

Be kind to yourself.

That sounds simple, but it’s harder than it looks—especially in a world that rewards speed, productivity and “always on” energy. We’re often quick to extend compassion to others but incredibly slow to give it to ourselves.

But the best leaders, teammates, and innovators I know all have one thing in common — they give themselves grace.

✨ Grace to learn without expecting perfection overnight.
✨ Grace to make mistakes without labeling everything as a failure.
✨ Grace to rest without feeling guilty.
✨ Grace to be human.

Here’s the truth—growth doesn’t happen in perfectly polished moments. It happens in the messy middle when projects don’t go to plan, when feedback stings, when we try something bold and it falls flat. That’s where the learning is. That’s where resilience gets built. 💪 

Listen, there are times when I get stuck on the lows and replay everything I should have done differently. But the emotional heaviness that comes with being your harshest critic is like mental quicksand — it traps your energy and rarely leads to anything productive.

Self-kindness isn’t about lowering the bar. It’s about creating the space we need to keep showing up—clear-minded, energized and ready to do our best work.

So here’s your gentle reminder:
✅ Celebrate the small wins—they add up.
✅ Don’t let one hard day erase months of progress.
✅ Speak to yourself the way you would to a friend who’s struggling.

Kindness fuels confidence. Grace fuels growth. And both are essential—not just for our careers, but for our well-being.

What’s one way you’ve given yourself grace recently?

A generic landing page does not automatically mean an AI slop website.

Yes, we’ve all seen the familiar patterns:
1. Big headline.
2. Purple gradient.
3. Bento-grid features.
4. “Revolutionize your workflow with AI.”

They can make a website feel generic but visual similarity alone tells us very little about the actual product.

A templated landing page can still lead to a useful, reliable product that solves a real problem. Meanwhile, a beautifully designed and completely original website can still hide broken features, fake testimonials, and little real value.

The better question is not:
“Does this website look AI-generated?”

It is:
“If we remove the polished visuals, does this product still provide meaningful value to a specific user?”

AI-assisted development is not the problem. The problem begins when generated output is treated as the finished product without enough judgment, testing, originality, or understanding of the user.

Generic design is a branding problem.

AI slop is a substance problem.

Store vs Warehouse vs Logistics: What Is the Difference?
Many people think Store, Warehouse, and Logistics mean the same thing, but they are completely different functions in the supply chain. Understanding these differences is essential for anyone working in inventory, warehouse operations, or logistics.

 📦 Store vs Warehouse vs Logistics – Do You Know the Difference?
Many people use these three terms interchangeably, but each has a unique role in the supply chain.
🔹 Store – Ensures materials are available for daily operations. Its focus is stock availability and issuing materials when needed.
🔹 Warehouse – Manages inventory efficiently through receiving, storage, picking, packing, and dispatch while maintaining high inventory accuracy.
🔹 Logistics – Connects the entire supply chain by transporting goods from suppliers to warehouses and finally to customers—on time and at the lowest possible cost.
From my 10+ years of experience in warehouse operations, I've learned that supply chain success doesn't depend on just one function. It depends on how well Store, Warehouse, and Logistics work together.
✅ Store keeps operations running.
✅ Warehouse keeps inventory under control.
✅ Logistics keeps business moving.
When these three functions are aligned, businesses achieve higher productivity, lower costs, and better customer satisfaction.

📊 Understanding the Balance Sheet: A Snapshot of a Company's Financial Health

One of the most important financial statements every finance student and professional should understand is the Balance Sheet.

A balance sheet provides a snapshot of what a company owns (Assets), owes (Liabilities), and the owner's share (Equity) at a specific point in time.

Here's a simple way to understand it:

✅ Assets – Resources owned by the company, such as cash, inventory, buildings, and equipment.

✅ Liabilities – Financial obligations the company needs to pay, such as loans, creditors, and outstanding expenses.

✅ Owner's Equity – The owner's investment in the business after deducting liabilities from assets.

The basic accounting equation is:

Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity

Why is a Balance Sheet important?

📌 It helps assess a company's financial position.
📌 It supports investment and lending decisions.
📌 It shows how efficiently a company manages its resources.
📌 It is one of the key financial statements used by managers, investors, and analysts.

As an MBA Finance graduate, I believe understanding financial statements is the foundation of making informed business decisions.

A strong resume does more than list your experience—it should quickly show employers why you're a great fit for the role. 📄✨

Here are 6 common mistakes that can reduce the impact of your resume:

❌ 1. Using a Generic Resume
🎯 Tailor your resume to the specific position and employer instead of sending the same version everywhere.

❌ 2. Writing a Weak Profile Summary
📝 Your opening summary should clearly communicate your experience, strengths, and career value.

❌ 3. Listing Responsibilities Without Achievements
🏆 Don't just say what you were responsible for. Highlight results, improvements, and measurable accomplishments.

❌ 4. Poor Formatting and Too Much Text
📋 Keep your resume clean, structured, and easy to scan. Recruiters often review resumes quickly.

❌ 5. Missing Job-Specific Keywords
🔑 Use relevant skills and keywords from the job description—especially important when resumes are screened by ATS systems.

❌ 6. Grammar, Spelling, and Formatting Errors
✅ Small mistakes can make a resume look careless. Always proofread before submitting.

💡 Remember: Your resume should be easy to read, relevant to the role, and focused on achievements—not just duties.

👉 Before applying for your next job, take a few minutes to review your resume against these six points.

📌 Make Your Resume Easy to Read. Hard to Reject.

Inversión extranjera directa: una inyección de confianza para la economía dominicana

La República Dominicana continúa consolidándose como uno de los destinos más atractivos para la inversión en América Latina y el Caribe. El crecimiento sostenido de la Inversión Extranjera Directa (IED) refleja algo más que la entrada de capitales: representa confianza en la estabilidad económica, el potencial productivo y las oportunidades de desarrollo que ofrece el país.

Detrás de cada inversión existen nuevas empresas, expansión de operaciones, generación de empleos, transferencia de conocimientos y oportunidades para fortalecer sectores estratégicos. Turismo, zonas francas, energía, tecnología, logística, manufactura y bienes raíces figuran entre las áreas que continúan captando el interés de inversionistas internacionales.

Este dinamismo también plantea importantes desafíos. El crecimiento de la inversión debe traducirse en mayor productividad, empleos de calidad, desarrollo regional y encadenamientos con las pequeñas y medianas empresas locales. La meta no debe limitarse a atraer más capital, sino a lograr que ese capital genere un impacto sostenible y ampliamente distribuido.

Para mantener esta trayectoria, será fundamental continuar fortaleciendo la seguridad jurídica, la transparencia institucional, la formación del talento humano y la infraestructura. Un entorno competitivo y predecible permite que la inversión no solo llegue, sino que permanezca, se expanda y contribuya al crecimiento de largo plazo.

La inversión extranjera directa es una señal clara de confianza, pero también una oportunidad estratégica. El reto para la República Dominicana consiste en convertir ese flujo de capital en innovación, competitividad y bienestar para más ciudadanos.

El crecimiento de la inversión es una buena noticia. Transformarla en desarrollo sostenible será la verdadera medida del éxito.

[AstraZeneca](https://linkedin.com/company/astrazeneca) Bets Big on [Dizal Pharmaceutical](https://linkedin.com/company/dizal-pharma)'s Lung 🫁 #Cancer Drug, #Zegfrovy®

[AstraZeneca](https://linkedin.com/company/astrazeneca) just made a major move in #oncology, agreeing to pay $600 million upfront💰 for global rights to China's [Dizal Pharmaceutical](https://linkedin.com/company/dizal-pharma)’s lung cancer drug, #Sunvozertinib, also known as Zegfrovy®.

The deal sent shares of Dizal(688192.SS) up⏫️ 20% today!

Sunvozertinib is a next-generation, orally bioavailable, irreversible EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor(TKI) that "selectively targets" exon20ins-mutant EGFR.

Thus, Zegfrovy® is an oral targeted therapy.

It is approved in both the U.S.🇺🇲 and China🇨🇳 for adults with locally advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer(#NSCLC)harbouring a rare genetic #mutation.

For these patients, first-line treatment has largely been limited to #chemotherapy!

That could change now👏

In a late-stage multinational trial of 324 patients, Sunvozertinib delivered a median progression-free survival(PFS) of 10.3 months vs. 7.5 months for chemotherapy👏

While overall survival(OS) data is still maturing, the results point to a meaningful clinical benefit in a hard-to-treat population.

About 77% of all lung cancers are non-small cell, per the [American Cancer Society](https://linkedin.com/company/american-cancer-society), and targeted options remain limited for this specific mutation.

Under the #agreement, [AstraZeneca](https://linkedin.com/company/astrazeneca) gains global development and commercialization rights. Dizal is also eligible for up to $900 million in additional payments tied to clinical, regulatory, and sales #milestones.

With this agreement, [AstraZeneca](https://linkedin.com/company/astrazeneca) will bring a differentiated, oral targeted treatment to patients with limited options.

The #deal also highlights China’s growing role in global drug #innovation.

Dizal, founded in 2017, reported ∼576 million yuan ($85M) in Sunvozertinib revenue in 2025, up 85% YoY⏫️

With [AstraZeneca](https://linkedin.com/company/astrazeneca)’s scale now behind it, the drug could now reach far more patients worldwide👏🌎👏

A generic landing page does not automatically mean an AI slop website.

Yes, we’ve all seen the familiar patterns:
1. Big headline.
2. Purple gradient.
3. Bento-grid features.
4. “Revolutionize your workflow with AI.”

They can make a website feel generic but visual similarity alone tells us very little about the actual product.

A templated landing page can still lead to a useful, reliable product that solves a real problem. Meanwhile, a beautifully designed and completely original website can still hide broken features, fake testimonials, and little real value.

The better question is not:
“Does this website look AI-generated?”

It is:
“If we remove the polished visuals, does this product still provide meaningful value to a specific user?”

AI-assisted development is not the problem. The problem begins when generated output is treated as the finished product without enough judgment, testing, originality, or understanding of the user.

Generic design is a branding problem.

AI slop is a substance problem.

Store vs Warehouse vs Logistics: What Is the Difference?
Many people think Store, Warehouse, and Logistics mean the same thing, but they are completely different functions in the supply chain. Understanding these differences is essential for anyone working in inventory, warehouse operations, or logistics.

 📦 Store vs Warehouse vs Logistics – Do You Know the Difference?
Many people use these three terms interchangeably, but each has a unique role in the supply chain.
🔹 Store – Ensures materials are available for daily operations. Its focus is stock availability and issuing materials when needed.
🔹 Warehouse – Manages inventory efficiently through receiving, storage, picking, packing, and dispatch while maintaining high inventory accuracy.
🔹 Logistics – Connects the entire supply chain by transporting goods from suppliers to warehouses and finally to customers—on time and at the lowest possible cost.
From my 10+ years of experience in warehouse operations, I've learned that supply chain success doesn't depend on just one function. It depends on how well Store, Warehouse, and Logistics work together.
✅ Store keeps operations running.
✅ Warehouse keeps inventory under control.
✅ Logistics keeps business moving.
When these three functions are aligned, businesses achieve higher productivity, lower costs, and better customer satisfaction.
