📊 Understanding the Balance Sheet: A Snapshot of a Company's Financial Health

One of the most important financial statements every finance student and professional should understand is the Balance Sheet.

A balance sheet provides a snapshot of what a company owns (Assets), owes (Liabilities), and the owner's share (Equity) at a specific point in time.

Here's a simple way to understand it:

✅ Assets – Resources owned by the company, such as cash, inventory, buildings, and equipment.

✅ Liabilities – Financial obligations the company needs to pay, such as loans, creditors, and outstanding expenses.

✅ Owner's Equity – The owner's investment in the business after deducting liabilities from assets.

The basic accounting equation is:

Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity

Why is a Balance Sheet important?

📌 It helps assess a company's financial position.
📌 It supports investment and lending decisions.
📌 It shows how efficiently a company manages its resources.
📌 It is one of the key financial statements used by managers, investors, and analysts.

As an MBA Finance graduate, I believe understanding financial statements is the foundation of making informed business decisions.

🚨 Common Resume Mistakes You Should Avoid

A strong resume does more than list your experience—it should quickly show employers why you're a great fit for the role. 📄✨

Here are 6 common mistakes that can reduce the impact of your resume:

❌ 1. Using a Generic Resume
🎯 Tailor your resume to the specific position and employer instead of sending the same version everywhere.

❌ 2. Writing a Weak Profile Summary
📝 Your opening summary should clearly communicate your experience, strengths, and career value.

❌ 3. Listing Responsibilities Without Achievements
🏆 Don't just say what you were responsible for. Highlight results, improvements, and measurable accomplishments.

❌ 4. Poor Formatting and Too Much Text
📋 Keep your resume clean, structured, and easy to scan. Recruiters often review resumes quickly.

❌ 5. Missing Job-Specific Keywords
🔑 Use relevant skills and keywords from the job description—especially important when resumes are screened by ATS systems.

❌ 6. Grammar, Spelling, and Formatting Errors
✅ Small mistakes can make a resume look careless. Always proofread before submitting.

💡 Remember: Your resume should be easy to read, relevant to the role, and focused on achievements—not just duties.

👉 Before applying for your next job, take a few minutes to review your resume against these six points.

Inversión extranjera directa: una inyección de confianza para la economía dominicana

La República Dominicana continúa consolidándose como uno de los destinos más atractivos para la inversión en América Latina y el Caribe. El crecimiento sostenido de la Inversión Extranjera Directa (IED) refleja algo más que la entrada de capitales: representa confianza en la estabilidad económica, el potencial productivo y las oportunidades de desarrollo que ofrece el país.

Detrás de cada inversión existen nuevas empresas, expansión de operaciones, generación de empleos, transferencia de conocimientos y oportunidades para fortalecer sectores estratégicos. Turismo, zonas francas, energía, tecnología, logística, manufactura y bienes raíces figuran entre las áreas que continúan captando el interés de inversionistas internacionales.

Este dinamismo también plantea importantes desafíos. El crecimiento de la inversión debe traducirse en mayor productividad, empleos de calidad, desarrollo regional y encadenamientos con las pequeñas y medianas empresas locales. La meta no debe limitarse a atraer más capital, sino a lograr que ese capital genere un impacto sostenible y ampliamente distribuido.

Para mantener esta trayectoria, será fundamental continuar fortaleciendo la seguridad jurídica, la transparencia institucional, la formación del talento humano y la infraestructura. Un entorno competitivo y predecible permite que la inversión no solo llegue, sino que permanezca, se expanda y contribuya al crecimiento de largo plazo.

La inversión extranjera directa es una señal clara de confianza, pero también una oportunidad estratégica. El reto para la República Dominicana consiste en convertir ese flujo de capital en innovación, competitividad y bienestar para más ciudadanos.

El crecimiento de la inversión es una buena noticia. Transformarla en desarrollo sostenible será la verdadera medida del éxito.

AI ambition is everywhere, but how do organizations turn it into real results? 

For me, the answer is clear - invest in people as much as technology.

That was the focus of my discussion last Monday at London Tech Week with Matt Prebble, CEO of Accenture UK & Ireland, and Patricia Clarke, Tech Editor at The Observer, discussing how bp is reshaping for growth. 

My biggest takeaway is that AI adoption is not primarily a technology challenge. It’s also a people challenge. 

AI is not new to bp, we have used it for years to help improve safety, performance and efficiency. What has changed is the pace and scale, and this changes the skills conversation completely.

At bp, we are investing in building those capabilities from the c-suite to the frontline, helping people use AI to challenge, redesign and improve how work gets done every day. We are building a simpler, more valuable bp and the more skills we put into the hands of our people, the more effective and efficient we become.

As these tools become more powerful, the human skills matter more, not less. Critical and strategic thinking, adaptability, real-world experience and judgement turn AI capability into delivery. The organizations that perform best will be those where people feel confident to stay curious, try new things, challenge outputs and keep learning. 
 
Because if we can help people learn faster, we can adapt faster. And in a world moving at this pace, that is what will turn AI ambition into real business value.

This year’s Social Mobility Day theme #StoriesMatter speaks to me.
 
My route into work was through an apprenticeship. It wasn’t obvious, and it wasn’t always easy. What made the difference were people who took a chance on me, guided me, and helped me see beyond where I started. Many of them are still in my life today.

That’s why stories matter.

Across bp, colleagues have been sharing theirs - from teams in the UK, Kuala Lumpur, Pune and the US, as well as students visiting our offices for Social Mobility Day. It’s been a powerful reminder that there is no single path.

We often make assumptions about how people got to where they are. Those assumptions can hold people back. When we share our stories - and really listen - we start to break those barriers. We help others see what might be possible. And we create space for voices that might otherwise go unheard, because not everyone asks for help.

For me, social mobility is about more than access - it’s about belonging. It’s about being able to say, “I belong on the other side,” and having the confidence to include yourself in spaces where you might not initially see people like you.

I believe deeply that where you start should not define where you end up. Talent is everywhere - opportunity is not.

I’m proud of the work we’re doing at bp, including our Social Mobility business resource group, which has brought colleagues together today across the company. But there is more to do. We need to widen access, notice those who may not speak up, and continue to create space for every voice.

Tough times have a way of sharpening your perspective and reshaping how you think about resilience.

This was me, living with breast cancer in 2020. Having since recovered, I realised it was never about speed - and neither was reaching Everest Base Camp. Both were journeys where mindset mattered and where the harder moments called for focus and resolve.

Treatment taught me to slow down, respect my limits, and keep moving when progress felt uncertain. Training for the trek felt much the same. Some days were strong. Others were simply about showing up and putting one foot in front of the other.

What stayed with me was how similar recovery and the climb really are. Resilience isn’t about pushing nonstop. It’s about good judgement, staying clear on what matters, and keeping things moving when the road gets harder.

I’m deeply grateful to my family, especially my son, Finlay, who joined the trek, and to the friends and volunteers who supported me along the way. None of this is ever done alone.

For me, resilience shows up in how I lead day to day. Staying grounded. Making thoughtful choices. And sometimes, when the moment comes, resilience is about finishing strong.

Proud to see Lloyds Banking Group recognised as one of LinkedIn's top companies, and the highest-ranked UK bank. For me, it reflects something simple: meaningful work, future-ready skills, and purpose you can see in action. Here’s why.

Curiosity doesn’t fade with experience. If anything, it becomes more important over time. I had a really thoughtful conversation this week about careers, curiosity and what actually keeps people motivated – and it left me reflecting on a few things.

Curiosity still matters: probably more than ever. 

Not curiosity for curiosity’s sake, but that instinct to ask questions, look beyond your own role, and really understand people, context and what’s changing around you. Especially now, when AI can take on so much of the “task” work.

Purpose is what gets people out of bed – and keeps them coming back.

People don’t come to work just for tasks or titles. They come for learning, connection and to feel part of something that matters. If organisations want the next generation to show up, stay curious and keep growing, we have to create cultures that don’t knock that instinct out of them.

Careers aren’t neat.

They’re built on a mix of hard work, capability and opportunity – and having the confidence to say yes, or ask the question. If you don’t ask, you don’t get. That hasn’t changed – and I don’t think it ever will.

And while AI will change how we work, it won’t replace what matters most.

The first mile – starting a conversation, spotting an idea, being brave enough to reach out. And the final mile – building trust, relationships and follow‑through. That’s still human territory.

One final reflection: leadership only works if you stay close to the real work.

If you’re not spending time with the people doing the job, listening to what’s working and what isn’t, it’s very easy to slip into assumption rather than reality.

A big thank you to Jackson Parsons and Meagen Burnett, CFO at Schroders, for such an open and honest discussion – and to the Richmond L&D Forum for creating the space for these conversations.

Today, as we celebrate the progress women have made around the world for #IWD, I can’t help but think about the girls and women who are living through conflict, not on the margins of the story, but right at the centre of it. Across conflicts around the world, women are among those most affected by wars they did not choose.

A few grounding facts, hard to read, but important to face, drawn from the work of the UN and its humanitarian agencies:

• In Afghanistan, women are now excluded from almost every part of public life. Following new restrictions in late 2024, no girls are expected to be in secondary education, according to UN reporting, making Afghanistan the only country where this is the case.

• In Gaza, UN Women reports that more than a million women are facing catastrophic hunger, reflecting the devastating humanitarian impact these sorts of conflicts have on civilians.

• Across parts of West and Central Africa affected by violence and climate shocks, women and children make up around 80% of refugees and asylum seekers, according to UNHCR.

• In Ukraine, UN agencies report that nearly 6.7 million women need humanitarian assistance, gender‑based violence has increased significantly, and years of progress on equality have been rolled back by the war.

Behind every statistic is a human story, lives shaped by disrupted childhoods, lost education, forced displacement and the quiet, relentless work of holding families and communities together.

So today, alongside celebration, I’m asking us to pause and think of them. To notice. To care. And to stand with women who are still fighting for safety, dignity and opportunity.

Happy International Women's Day to all.

Be curious, a continuous learner. Lean into the discomfort, hone critical thinking and communication skills.

Over the last year it has been clear to me that these are some of the core capabilities needed to succeed as we become a more AI-enabled workforce. They are just as relevant as I think about my kids trying to get to grips with learning in the age of AI.

One critical need, which the ‘Count on It: AI, Numeracy and Social Mobiliy’ report conducted by @Policy Connect rightly calls out - is the need for numeracy.

It was terrific to participate in a panel in the House of Commons this week, as part of the National Numeracy Council’s discussion of the findings of the report, which include:

- Numeracy is a foundational condition for critical AI engagement - AI outputs are based on probabilistic reasoning and statistical patterns shape responses - this makes numeracy a core skill in the critical thinking needed to interpret outcomes.

💡Yet, only 25 % of respondents in the report recognised numeracy as a prerequisite for using AI effectively

- Risk of over reliance - 77% of respondents who used AI trust outputs to be accurate - without key numeracy and critical thinking skills outputs will be used in error. 

⚖️instead of levelling the playing field with its ability to significantly broaden access to information, guidance and opportunity, AI could serve to tilt it further.

In my role as Chair of the LSEG Foundation we see numeracy as a confidence issue as much as a capability issue - through our charity partners we hear how many young adults avoid maths-related tasks completely, and have ‘maths anxiety’.

What’s clear is that to make AI a genuine driver of social mobility, three things matter:

✔️access to the tools themselves
✔️Human not in the loop as much as ‘at the Helm’ : in identifying where to delegate to the AI and the confidence to apply it to value driving use cases
✔️the capability to apply critical thinking to use and challenge outcomes

If we don’t build those capabilities more broadly in our workplaces, schools and societies we will be reinforcing our existing inequalities.

Highly recommend a look at the report below ⬇️ and the five recommendations for employers, policy makers and educators.

Today is World Mental Health Day 🌎 . It’s a moment to pause and reflect on something that affects us all—our mental wellbeing.

This year’s theme, “Access to Services – Mental Health in Catastrophes and Emergencies”, reminds us that mental health support is not a luxury—it’s essential, especially in times of crisis.

The bombardment and mental toll of wars, natural disasters, personal loss, and the uncertainty and complexity of daily life are omnipresent.


Did you know?
1 in 8 people globally live with a mental health condition.
After major disasters, up to 30% of survivors may experience depression, anxiety, or PTSD.
At work, 51% of employees fear that speaking about mental health could harm their career.

But we also know—because research has shown—that every conversation, every act of kindness, every moment of listening can make a difference.
I want to help others regain their sparkle, feel safe to say “I’m not okay,” and find ways to access the support they need. This is what building a culture of care is all about.

Because behind every title, every frown, and every smile is a person who might just need an act of kindness and a moment of compassion.

If we all commit to checking in on one another, we’re more likely to catch each other when we fall.

#WorldMentalHealthDay #CompassGroup #MentalHealthMatters #KindnessIsStrength

It was a pleasure to join the Crisil Client Dinner last week and spend the evening in conversation with Crisil's leadership, Board members and global clients about the changes reshaping finance. We were treated to a fascinating opening conversation with England cricketer and Former Captain Jos Buttler, expertly moderated by Gaurav Ahuja, who shared leadership lessons from his remarkable career. A hard act to follow. 
  
Building on the themes in the opening conversation, I was delighted to be part of a fireside chat, hosted by Gaurav Arora, which covered everything from the forces transforming banking and the broader financial services industry to AI and the changing nature of work. Throughout our conversation, we reflected on the fact that today’s businesses are not facing a singular trend, but several structural shifts that are converging all at once – from the emergence of a multi-aligned world to rising wealth participation in new markets. 
  
We also discussed how organisations need to prepare for a future where work becomes more fluid and technology increasingly complements human capability. Reflecting some of Jos’s earlier comments, we discussed the changing role of leaders, who are not just responsible for encouraging performance ‘here and now’ but also responsible for steering the course and helping their teams build longer term capabilities, particularly ones which will evolve alongside AI.  
  
My view remains that the organisations that will thrive are those that bring together technology, talent and trusted relationships. AI may be accelerating change, but judgement, curiosity, adaptability and human connection will continue to remain highly relevant. 
  
Thank you to the Crisil team for the invitation and for bringing together such a thoughtful group of leaders and perspectives. I always leave these conversations optimistic about the future and the opportunities ahead when we combine innovation with investment in people.

In today’s macro-environment, sometimes staying ahead is not only about reacting faster but also understanding how the global economic system itself is changing.

This is a theme that keeps coming up in conversations with clients and colleagues, and it’s what inspired our Group Public and Regulatory Affairs team to produce its latest report on the Top Five Policy Issues shaping public policy in 2026.

We’re moving into a phase where change is no longer gradual. It's structural and it’s happening in real time. At the centre of this shift are five interconnected trends that are reshaping how organisations think about growth, resilience and long-term positioning:

➡️ The rebalancing of power as global relationships become more dynamic and less predictable
➡️ Technology adoption and integration as AI and digital assets move from optional tools to strategic priorities, with real value coming from how we build the skills to use them well
➡️ The race for resources as energy, critical minerals and infrastructure increasingly shape economic and security decisions
➡️ Societal divisions influencing policy direction and making long-term reform more complex
➡️ Global governance shifting from traditional frameworks to more issue-based approaches

These forces are not arriving sequentially, and they cannot be managed in silos. The organisations that lead through this period are those that understand these shifts not as a constraint to manage, but as a strategic input.

So the question for leaders is: how are you adapting your strategy when the system itself is evolving in real time? I would be very interested to hear how others are thinking about these changes. The full paper is linked in the comments if useful as you reflect on what comes next.

An energising few days at the Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity, packed with conversations on leadership, creativity and the role businesses and organisations can play in creating meaningful, lasting change.

It was a privilege to join Naomi Schiff alongside Jayathma Wickramanayake, Susie Wolff, Kate (Pratt) Theobald and Lisa O'Keefe MBE at Cannes LIONS Sport for Beyond Campaigns: Rethinking How We Keep Girls in Sport.

The facts are well known: 94% of women in C-suite roles played sport growing up, yet by age 14, girls drop out at twice the rate of boys. We know the challenge. The real question is why progress has been slower than it should be.

For me, the answer is simple. Campaigns can spark awareness, but lasting change comes from sustained action. Creating more opportunities for women and girls through sport requires businesses, sporting organisations, policymakers and communities to work together with a shared ambition and a long-term commitment, grounded in a shared framework.

At Standard Chartered, this is why initiatives like our GOAL accelerator programme in several of our markets, Play On with Liverpool Football Club and our partnership with F1 ACADEMY matter. They are about much more than sport. They are about connecting people to opportunity, helping women and girls realise their potential, and creating pathways for them to thrive. This is why we’re working together, to help turn intent into impact, at scale.

I also had the opportunity to sit down with Ashish Verma at Bloomberg  Media Studios. We spoke about leadership in a period of rapid change, and one idea stayed with me: the leaders who will make the biggest difference over the next decade won’t be those who seek to control every outcome, but those who bring people together around a shared purpose.

Because whether we’re talking about the future of work or the future of sport, our biggest challenges cannot be solved in isolation.

Thank you to everyone who contributed to these conversations. Much more to come.

An exciting moment for us at Standard Chartered with the launch of our first Agentic AI colleague-facing solution, focused on new-hire onboarding. This marks an important milestone in how we are using AI to improve our colleague’s experience by fundamentally redesigning how work gets done. 
 
By embedding AI, we are simplifying a complex journey, improving the experience for new joiners, and reducing onboarding effort for hiring managers by an estimated 35% of the time they would otherwise spend on these tasks. Crucially, humans remain firmly in the loop — working in partnership with AI, which takes on the repetitive and administrative coordination so colleagues can focus on judgement, problem‑solving, and human connection.
 
This approach is a direct response to what we have learned through our work on workforce and operating-model redesign. When AI is layered onto existing processes without redesigning the work, 95% of organisations see zero ROI from AI investments. By contrast, leading AI organisations are twice as likely to redesign workflows to deliberately integrate human and machine capabilities. These insights shaped our decision to breakdown jobs into tasks, deciding what should be done by humans versus machines, and rebuilding the workflow around that split. 
 
This points to a broader shift - jobs matter less than tasks and skills. As agentic AI application increases, the most valuable skills will be those that sit alongside technology, such as digital fluency, human-AI collaboration, and the ability to interpret and improve outcomes. That is why we are linking this work to our focus on skills of the future and Global Learning Week (which starts today), building capacity as we redesign work. 
 
There is opportunity for leaders to move beyond experimenting with AI, and to redesign the workforce within organisations where people and machines work together intentionally - not by accident. 
 
#FutureOfWork #AgenticAI #WorkforceTransformation

Here's the context that makes it essential reading right now. China represents roughly 15% of global trade, yet the RMB accounts for less than 3.1% of global payments and just 1.9% of global reserves. That structural gap is narrowing, and the drivers this time are durable — rooted in real-economy demand rather than short-term policy cycles.

The infrastructure to support this is firmly in place, liquidity pools are deepening, and onshore and offshore markets are becoming increasingly connected. For corporates with China-linked exposure, this is no longer a theoretical conversation — your supply chains, procurement flows and revenue streams are already embedded in Asia-centred trade networks, whether or not your treasury framework has caught up.

Helping our clients navigate exactly that kind of complexity — with the expertise, the network and the long-term commitment to the markets where they operate — is what Standard Chartered is here to do.

I’ve been reflecting on how quickly geopolitical developments move from headlines to markets and real economic trade‑offs. In a recent conversation on our podcast, Standard Chartered's Eric Robertsen and Madhur Jha explored a key question - is the oil shock arising from the Middle East conflict more likely to fuel inflation pressures, or deepen growth concerns? They also unpacked how the Strait of Hormuz closure is affecting not just energy supplies, but other critical sectors, and what this means across regions, economies, and asset classes. 
 
What we’re seeing right now feels less like a single event and more like a multi‑step adjustment. Even if there is de‑escalation, it may not follow a smooth or predictable path. Ongoing uncertainty around key routes like the Strait of Hormuz matters, not just for oil prices, but for the wider global economy. 
 
A few patterns stand out. First, this is about more than energy prices. Oil and LNG are the most visible channels, but the Middle East is deeply embedded in global supply chains. Disruption can extend into petrochemicals, with knock‑on effects across multiple sectors. Where infrastructure has been damaged, especially LNG facilities, the economic impact can last for years. 
 
Second, markets are reacting through an inflation lens, but growth risks sit just behind it. Energy prices tend to hit inflation expectations quickly, and we’ve seen a shift away from expected rate cuts in some markets. History suggests that when price shocks persist, there is a bigger hit to growth that unfolds gradually over several quarters rather than all at once. 
 
Third, diversification is proving more challenging than expected.  Some traditional safe havens assets have not behaved as they typically do, which complicates risk management and portfolio construction. In this environment, liquidity and judgement matter as much as models. 
 
For me, the key takeaway is a familiar one. Periods like this reward clarity of thinking and patience. Not every signal deserves an immediate response. For businesses (and leaders), this is a reminder that steady long‑term thinking is a competitive advantage when uncertainty rises.

It’s a reminder that transformation isn’t just about the “hardware” - the models, tools, and infrastructure - but the “software”: how we think, decide, and lead differently in response.

The real value of AI isn’t in replacing judgment, but in sharpening it. That balance between machine-led precision and human-led accountability is where the most meaningful transformation takes shape.

This week marks Neurodiversity Awareness Week, a timely reminder of how important it is to recognise that we all work, think, learn, and process information in different ways. 
 
To mark the week, we gathered colleagues across our markets to discuss a fundamental truth: creating a culture where people of all abilities thrive shouldn’t be complex, and it doesn’t require each of us to become an expert in every type of disability – it simply requires us to be curious and open minded. 

As the Global Sponsor of the Standard Chartered Ability Colleague Community, I was thrilled to join Disha Mehta and Ollie Thorn alongside colleagues in London to discuss how the experience of visible and invisible disability can impact leadership. My key takeaways from our session:

​1️⃣ Stop fixing humans, start fixing environments - we spend too much time trying to make people fit a mold. Real change happens when we design environments that accommodate everyone from the start.

​2️⃣ The Power of Lived Experience - having the “ingredients” for a good culture isn't enough. We must amplify the voices of those with diverse lived experiences. Their stories are the catalysts for true transformation.

​3️⃣ Create Safe Spaces - when we build forums where people can share openly, we bridge the gap between "initiative" and "impact."

​4️⃣ The Long Game - we often overestimate what we can do in one year, but underestimate what we can accomplish in ten. Changing the world doesn't happen overnight, but it starts with the questions we ask today.

​Our discussion reinforced my view that inclusion isn't a box to check; it's a muscle we build every day by active listening and driving small impactful change with consistency.

#Inclusion

When International Women's Day comes around, I find myself reflecting on a simple but powerful truth: progress is never accidental. It’s the result of deliberate choices, sustained commitment, and — critically — the courage to be transparent about where we still fall short.
 
IWD is a timely reminder that equality is not a destination. It is a discipline and at Standard Chartered, this discipline runs through everything we do — for our colleagues, our clients, and our communities.
 
Since signing the Women in Finance Charter in 2016, we have increased women's representation in senior leadership from 25% to over 33%. We introduced equalised parental leave of at least 20 weeks globally; became one of the first global institutions to offer menopause-related medical cover; and in last year, while many others pulled back on flexible working, we leaned in — trusting our people and their leaders to find what works. Our Inclusion Index stands at over 80%, reflecting a culture where colleagues feel heard, valued, and empowered.
 
Through SC WIN — our Women's International Network — we have committed to USD 1 billion in financing for women-led businesses globally by 2028. Since launching in 2022, the programme has already delivered USD540 million to women entrepreneurs across seven markets.
 
And through the Standard Chartered Foundation, programmes such Goal, Futuremakers, and Women in Tech continue to create pathways for young women — reaching hundreds of thousands of girls and young women across more than 20 countries with life skills, financial literacy, mentoring, and seed funding.
 
I am proud of what we have built. But I am equally honest about what remains. According to McKinsey & Company, globally women are underrepresented at every stage of the corporate pipeline and continue to be promoted to management roles in smaller numbers. The structural barriers — from discriminatory norms to funding gaps — are real and persistent.
 
That is why this work is not a programme. It is not a campaign. It is how we do business. Because when women thrive — in boardrooms, in businesses, in communities — everyone benefits. That is not aspiration. That is evidence.
 
Happy International Women's Day to the extraordinary women across our network — and to every ally who understands that equality is not a zero-sum game.

Recently I sat down with Brant Carson and Ishaan Seth from McKinsey & Company to share my reflections on what it really takes to drive lasting transformation — and why so often leaning towards conventional wisdom leaves transformation programmes missing the mark.
 
Transformation is one of the most overused words in business. Too often it describes a change programme with a start and end date, but real transformation requires you to hardwire new ways of working into how an organisation operates — not just declare them from the top. This is why the relationship between what I call the software, and hardware matters so much.
 
Most organisations instinctively reach for the hardware — the structural investments, the new processes, the governance mechanisms. And these matter, but the harder, and far too often underweighted, work is the software - the mindset shifts, the behavioural changes and the leadership culture that must carry the whole agenda. 
 
At Standard Chartered, the most powerful shift came when we stopped treating these as separate workstreams and started designing them together — mapping our processes, establishing clear accountability, and only then asking how to hardwire a culture of client centricity and innovation into the daily flow of work.
 
During the interview we also discussed the topic of AI, and my views that the barriers to adoption at scale are not technical in nature, but rather skills, leadership, and cultural challenges. The organisations that will lead in the race to capitalise on AI investments are those that build an environment where people engage with these tools confidently in the flow of their work, where human capabilities are augmented, not replaced by machines. As leaders, the responsibility to navigate this sits squarely with us.

Sometimes the blazer just has to feel too big at first…

This morning my youngest started senior school. His hand-me-down blazer from his big brother is at least a size too big, sleeves past his hands, shoulders a little too wide, but he wore it proudly even if I can tell he’s a bit anxious about what lies ahead. 

And it struck me that’s exactly how growth feels. Whether it’s starting a new role, taking on more responsibility, or stepping up as a leader, we rarely feel like the blazer fits on day one. It feels oversized, a little daunting, maybe even uncomfortable.

But over time, with encouragement, support and experience, we grow into it. Eventually, what once felt far too big becomes second nature.

At Man Group, we talk about high performance and culture but really, it’s about creating the kind of environment where people feel safe enough to try, supported enough to stumble, and encouraged enough to keep going until the blazer fits.

As leaders, our job isn’t to tailor the blazer to fit perfectly on day one. It’s to help people grow into it.

And as for my youngest, here’s hoping those sleeves won’t be covering his hands for too long.  He’s long overdue a growth spurt 😊 #leadership #mangroup #backtoschool

Last week was Neurodiversity Week, and it sparked some great conversations across Sage about how we make space for different ways of thinking at work. 

Many organisations, often unintentionally, still reward a fairly narrow style of contribution: thinking quickly, speaking confidently, and aligning fast. It works… but it also means we can miss valuable perspectives that don’t show up in that same way. 

Some of the most valuable insights I’ve seen don’t happen in the moment. They come later, from people who’ve had time to reflect, connect the dots, and really think things through. And when we make space for that, the quality of decisions improves. 

So maybe the question is less about getting everyone to contribute in the same way, and more about how we create the conditions for different thinking to shape outcomes. 

In reality, that often comes down to small things: 
💠  Giving people time to think before and after discussions 
💠  Making space for written input, not just verbal 
💠 Noticing whose perspective we haven’t heard yet 

As we move beyond Neurodiversity Week, that feels like the opportunity,   not just recognising difference, but actually designing for it. 

Because better thinking leads to better decisions.

Transformation is no longer a sequence of initiatives – it is happening everywhere, all at once.

At the German-speaking SAP User Group (DSAG e.V.) Personaltage event in Heidelberg, discussions showed: the shift toward an #AutonomousEnterprise is not about automation in the traditional sense. It is about intelligent assistants and agents that can operate end-to-end; augmented, orchestrated, and always with humans in the loop.

Three core takeaways I shared with the audience:
➖ Rewiring the organization for an AI-native world
We are moving from vertical silos to horizontal, end-to-end value streams. Agents operate across domains, so organizations must follow. This requires new operating models, orchestration layers, and hybrid teams where humans and AI collaborate seamlessly.
➖ Skills as the foundation of adaptability
With skill half-lives shrinking to 6–18 months, organizations need to become truly skill-based. “Learn to unlearn,” continuous reskilling, and real-time skill intelligence are becoming core capabilities for staying relevant.
➖ Human leadership remains central
In an Autonomous Enterprise, humans stay in the driver’s seat. Judgment, empathy, and ethical guardrails matter more, not less. The real challenge is to create the conditions for people to adopt, trust, and effectively work with AI.
 
During our joint panel, Hermann-Josef Haag, Board Member at DSAG, moderator Juliane Krampe, and I debated the following:
➖ Transformation is less a technology challenge, but increasingly a people, prioritization, and leadership challenge
➖ Organizations are managing multiple shifts at once: AI, architecture changes, workforce transformation, and external pressures
➖ The biggest pain points we see across customers are strategic workforce planning, skills transparency, and connecting data across HR, finance, and processes
➖ Progress requires clear target states and pragmatic, phased execution
➖ And most importantly: no organization can navigate this alone. Ecosystems and exchange are critical
 
From a broader SAP perspective, this reinforces our direction: enabling customers to run end-to-end business processes with integrated AI, data, and applications, while embedding people, skills, and change deeply into our transformation journey. Because ultimately, becoming an Autonomous Enterprise is about building adaptive organizations and ensuring employees have the enablement, support, and confidence to thrive in this new reality.

The pace will not slow down. The differentiator will be how deliberately we combine technology and human potential to shape what comes next.

#Sapphire 2026 is in the books – here are my three most important takeaways:
 
1. The Autonomous Enterprise: 
My biggest takeaways from SAP Sapphire this year was how clearly SAP articulated the next chapter of enterprise transformation: the Autonomous Enterprise - the beginning of better.
We clearly see the shift from AI as a productivity feature toward AI embedded into end-to-end business processes, grounded in trusted data, process expertise, and governance. And most importantly: this vision still keeps humans in the loop. Leadership, judgment, and cross-functional enterprise thinking become even more important in an AI-native world. Our new SAP Business AI Platform forms the basis for our vision of the future of business, where agents run the business and we can focus on what truly matters.
 
2. The SAP Experience Center: Innovation scales when everyone can contribute
Another highlight for me was visiting the SAP Experience Center. The colleagues on site showed in the most hands-on way, what it takes to move from competition to collaboration through the lens of a major global sports event. It was fascinating to see how SAP brings together data, applications, and AI through the autonomous enterprise so every company can operate as one and perform when it matters most.
 
3. Roger Federer: Excellence requires continuous reinvention
A very different (but equally memorable) moment was the Celebrity Keynote with #RogerFederer in conversation with our CEO Christian Klein. What stayed with me most was not the trophies, but the mindset behind a decades‑long career at the very top.
From a people perspective, three themes really stood out: #discipline, #resilience and #continuousgrowth. Federer talked about staying “coachable” even when you are already successful, being willing to keep learning, and having “fire in your belly and ice in your veins” when the pressure is highest. For me, this is exactly what we need to foster in our leaders and teams as work is being reshaped by AI and constant change.
One statistic he referenced hit home: even a legend like Federer only wins a bit more than half of the points he plays, yet he wins the majority of his matches. It is a powerful reminder that high performance cultures are not about avoiding mistakes, but about how quickly we reset, learn and move on from them. As People & Culture, our role is to create an environment where people feel safe enough to take smart risks, learn in the open and still bring their best under competitive conditions.

Finally, his focus on character and how you treat people really resonated with me. Excellence is not just what you deliver, but how you show up for others – on the court, in the office, and in our communities. That is the kind of leadership mindset we want to develop and reward.
 
Roger Federer demonstrated adaptability and reinvention as the real edge.

Leadership matters more than ever in moments like this. People need clarity on how work is changing, what new skills matter, and how AI can support them in their day-to-day work. That requires enablement at scale, continuous learning, and broad access to AI tools across the organization.

Because sustainable AI transformation happens when technology and people evolve together. #SAPSapphire

This is a remarkable shift: AI is not just supporting tasks. It is orchestrating outcomes across systems, teams, and physical operations. A simple way to think about it: It’s Monday morning. You start your job – and your AI teammate is already at work. Analyzing data, simulating scenarios, preparing decisions. What changes is not just speed. What changes is how work itself is designed.
 
But technology alone does not create value. The real question is whether we are redesigning work fast enough to unlock its full potential.
Because this transformation changes the fundamentals: We go from executing tasks to orchestrating outcomes, from rigid roles to dynamic skills, and from isolated tools to integrated, AI-supported processes.
 
That was the focus of our engaging discussion on the Center Stage: Skills are becoming the new currency of work. In a world where capabilities evolve continuously, the differentiator is not what people know today, but how quickly they learn, adapt, and apply.
 
For companies, this means: AI transformation is not a technology program. It is a work redesign and leadership challenge. Technology creates potential, but organizations need to learn how to turn it into impact.

The hardest part of AI transformation is not the technology. It is changing how work actually gets done.

Research points in the same direction: only a small share of AI value comes from the algorithms themselves. The bigger shift happens through people, processes and leadership; when organizations rethink roles, build new skills, and redesign how work happens.
That was at the heart of our first People & Culture Manager Day and the 2026 P&C Kick-Off at SAP, where colleagues from Mannheim, Prague, Bangalore, Newtown Square, Manila and many other locations came together to discuss what this means for the business and for P&C in particular.

Several insights stood out for me:
➔ Futurrist Ian Beacraft challenged us to think beyond automation: AI is reshaping how work is designed, how decisions are made, and which human capabilities create the most value.
➔ Kathi Enderes reinforced that the biggest barriers to AI impact are rarely technical, but organizational: skills, leadership, and the ability to translate technology into new ways of working.
➔ And in our panel with Pinar Dolen, Marielle Ehrmann, Dr. Magdalena Masluk-Meller Eric Goldstein and Ian, one point became very clear: if AI is reshaping the business, then People & Culture must transform too.

For us, that means three things in particular: rethinking how work happens with AI at the core, building new skills while unlearning outdated limits, and connecting more effectively across roles and teams to create impact faster.

For People & Culture, this is a defining moment. We’re not watching work change - we’re making it happen: redesigning the operating model, building the skills, and shaping the culture that turns AI into impact.

AI investments are at an all-time high. But a central question for leaders across industries is no longer whether to adopt AI. It’s how to build the capabilities to work with it.

Research gives us some insights on what matters most: Only 10% of AI value comes from algorithms, 20% from technology and data. But 70% comes from people, processes, and leadership. AI transformation is also a leadership and organizational transformational story, not just technology.

This perspective came alive this week at the Münchner Management Kolloquium at Technical University of Munich, where executives, scientists, and founders gathered under the theme “Bold Moves: Managing with Courage” to discuss how Europe can remain competitive in a rapidly changing technological landscape. In our panel with Britta Seeger, Bettina Dietsche, and Dane Molter, moderated by Prof. Dr. Claudia Peus, we explored how AI at work is crafting tomorrow.

One thing became clear: When technology evolves every few months, value no longer comes from what we know, but from how fast we adapt. That is why SAP is moving toward a skills‑led organization. We are entering a world where the shelf life of skills is shrinking dramatically, sometimes to just months.  
Therefore, the real challenge is not introducing AI. It is redesigning work, processes, operating models and skills at the speed AI evolves.

This year’s #MMK26 showed that we are ready for these bold moves. When companies, universities, and communities work together to prepare people for a world where humans and AI collaborate, we are not just ready for the future – we're actively designing it.

Zukunft made in Germany: 300 Millionen Euro für Technologie. Bis zu 700 neue Jobs bis 2030.   

Das bedeutet für uns: Chancen für Menschen. Perspektiven für die Region. Investition in Zukunftsfähigkeit.    

Wir investieren 300 Millionen Euro in Frankfurt und Offenbach, um Schlüsseltechnologien auszubauen, die die globale #Energiewende vorantreiben und die wachsende Nachfrage nach Infrastruktur für #KI-Rechenzentren bedienen können. Bis 2030 entstehen dabei bis zu 700 neue Arbeitsplätze – in Fertigung, Logistik und Verwaltung.   

Diese Investition ist nicht nur eine Frage von Technologie und Infrastruktur. Vielmehr geht es darum, echte Perspektiven zu schaffen – für die Menschen in der Region und für den Standort Deutschland:  

👥 Chancen für Menschen – Wir qualifizieren unsere Mitarbeitenden kontinuierlich weiter, damit sie die Kompetenzen entwickeln können, die im KI-Zeitalter gefragt sind. Denn nachhaltige #Beschäftigungsfähigkeit entsteht durch lebenslanges Lernen.   

📍 Perspektiven für die Region – Mit künftig drei Werken in Frankfurt und Offenbach schaffen wir Arbeitsplätze für unterschiedlichste Qualifikationen und stärken damit eine der wirtschaftlich wichtigsten Regionen Deutschlands.   

🚀 Investition in Zukunftsfähigkeit – Bei Siemens investieren wir nicht nur in Technologie, sondern ermöglichen es Menschen, diese Technologie mit Leidenschaft sinnvoll einzusetzen. Das macht uns stark – und stärkt die Wettbewerbsfähigkeit des Standorts #Deutschland.   

Für mich ist diese Investition ein klares Signal: Deutschland bleibt ein starker Industrie- und Technologiestandort – wenn Menschen mit Können, Neugier und Verantwortung handeln. Genau das macht den Unterschied – heute und morgen. 💪

Die Bitkom #TRANSFORM26 in Berlin war für mich ein wertvoller Impulsgeber: Wenn es um Transformation geht, müssen Politik und Wirtschaft eng zusammenrücken.

Im Dialog mit Bundesministerin Karin Prien (BMBFSFJ) und Marcel Fratzscher, Leiter des DIW, stand die zentrale Frage im Raum: „Diversity, Equity, Irrelevance: Kann unsere Wirtschaft auf Vielfalt verzichten?“

Die Antwort ist klar: Gerade für die digitale Transformation und zur Sicherung unserer Wettbewerbsfähigkeit ist #Vielfalt unverzichtbar. Sie ist kein „Nice-to-have“, sondern – in all ihren Facetten – ein entscheidender Wettbewerbsvorteil und ein Motor für #Innovation. Mehr Vielfalt, auch und insbesondere durch mehr Frauen, ist für die Wirtschaft essenziell.

Und mit Blick auf die demografischen Veränderungen in Deutschland wird deutlich: Wir können es uns als Gesellschaft und Wirtschaftsstandort nicht leisten, auf Erfahrung, Kompetenz und Engagement von Frauen zu verzichten.

Um mehr Frauen in Beschäftigung zu bringen, braucht es die richtigen Rahmenbedingungen. Ein zentraler Hebel ist dabei mehr #Flexibilität in der Arbeitszeit. Starre Vorgaben, wann und wie gearbeitet wird, sind in Zeiten von KI und digitaler Arbeit nicht mehr zeitgemäß. Die Einführung einer Wochenarbeitszeit kann hier ein wirkungsvolles Instrument sein: Sie ermöglicht es vielen Menschen, ihre Arbeitszeit auszuweiten und gleichzeitig Beruf und Privatleben selbstbestimmter zu vereinbaren.

Als einer der größten Arbeitgeber in Deutschland schaffen wir bereits heute – im Rahmen der gesetzlichen Möglichkeiten – vielfältige Optionen, um genau das zu unterstützen.

Doch klar ist auch: Ohne mutige politische Rahmenbedingungen und ein gemeinsames Verständnis von moderner Arbeit werden wir das vorhandene Potenzial nicht heben. Wenn wir Transformation wirklich gestalten wollen, müssen wir Vielfalt konsequent fördern, Flexibilität ermöglichen und die Arbeitswelt an die Realität der Menschen anpassen.

After Davos, action begins.

The conversations were valuable. Now comes the hard work of turning them into action.

In my latest article, I share a few reflections from the conversations I had with the people at Davos and what they signal for the road ahead.

I’d love to hear: what actions are you taking after #WEF26?

𝐈𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐀𝐈, 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐣𝐨𝐛, 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲?

That question framed our panel hosted by KPMG at AI House Davos during World Economic Forum. Together with May Habib and Alessandro De Luca, and moderated by Ashish Madan, we explored how AI and agentic systems are changing the very nature of work and organizations.

👉 A few reflections I keep coming back to:

1️⃣ What still defines a #job? 
A job is, fundamentally, a bundle of tasks or activities performed to achieve a certain outcome. What changes with AI is how these tasks are bundled –through automation or augmentation – and by whom they are performed: humans, machines, and agents. From an economic perspective, jobs are outcome-driven, balancing input and output. And yet, for us humans, a job is more than that. It is also about connection, identity, and purpose.

2️⃣ Transformation stands and falls with #people.
We tend to over-index on tools and technology, but 80% of change is behavioral and cultural. People’s engagement, rooted in trust and psychological safety, determines how fast organizations can really move.

3️⃣ #Leadership faces a paradox: “everything changes – and nothing changes.”
In the age of AI, it is the role of leaders to decide what business they are in and what purpose guides it. And they need to stay in control of what matters most. Leaders remain accountable for business models, quality, ethical decision-making, etc. The fundamentals – trust, empowerment, psychological safety and a growth mindset – matter just as much in the age of AI, if not more.

4️⃣ Which #organizations are we ultimately building?
AI will not lead to radical change unless we rethink our processes and operating models. The real question is which organizations we are ultimately building. This is not about incremental change, but about redesigning systems and enabling new ways of working. We need to be deliberate about where we automate tasks and where we augment human capability. And we must always keep humans in the loop – or even in the lead – because this is where human skills – such as judgment, contextual understanding, and purpose – remain essential.

I remain positive – yet not naive about AI. It can be a powerful enabler, helping us rethink industry, address demographic challenges, democratize knowledge, and protect our planet. 

In the end, the answers often do not lie in the technology alone.
They lie in the choices we make – and in how consciously and purposefully we apply technology, together.

It was a joy and a privilege to talk Circularity at the One Young World Summit in Munich, looking out to a room full of brilliant young leaders. I had the opportunity to engage on a topic that holds immense relevance for us today: how can we learn from circularity in nature and marry those eons of „R&D“ with today’s technology to get back to balance.
 
Life on this planet has always been circular. The ancient rhythm of cycles turns fallen leaves into soil, and returns a river’s water back to the sky. Everything in nature is interconnected. Every end is a new beginning.
And for the longest time, mankind lived by the rules and rhythm of nature - and its resourcefulness.

Yet with industrialization and globalization, we replaced the circle with a straight line - Take. Make. Dispose. The linear model seemed like a promise of growth and prosperity - but not for everyone, and it stretches our planet’s limits.

Now it's time to rebalance. We must decouple growth from resource consumption and change the operating model of the world from linear back to circular.

In this transformation to „circular by design“, technology is our most potent ally. AI and digital twins are enablers of breakthrough innovation in the digital world - with positive impact in the real world. 

Our wonderful young leaders and changemakers will be architects of renewal. If they - we all - choose the circle over the straight line. 

 So, let’s make the circle whole again – together!

80% of companies struggle to capture returns from their Gen AI investments, according to a 2025 McKinsey survey.

So how can we translate #GenAI potential into real #productivity?

There’s no simple answer – but #experimentation brings us closer.

The new Harvard Business Review article captures an important truth: the path to productivity isn’t linear. It’s a “J-curve” that requires a learning mindset and the courage to test, adapt, and scale what really works.

I’m pleased to see this approach, which we embrace at Siemens, featured in the article. For us, it’s experimentation that puts people at the center. In 2024, we ran the first test of our #IndustrialCopilot – a GenAI-powered shop-floor assistant – at our factory in Erlangen. Our maintenance engineers found it saved them time. But the real surprise came from our technicians – especially the more junior and less experienced staff – who said it helped them tackle complex issues more confidently, particularly on night shifts when no engineers were around.

This is what we mean by #TechnologywithPurpose: empowering people, enabling continuous learning, and ensuring digitalization delivers real value for our workforce and customers.

A big thank-you to my colleagues Nik von Hesler and Johannes Berndt for co-authoring this insightful piece and helping bring clarity to GenAI adoption for organizations.

#KI verändert unsere Arbeitswelt. Wir befähigen Menschen, sie mitzugestalten. Dafür braucht es neues Denken und Handeln.

Unsere Welt verändert sich rasant: Wir stehen am Beginn eines neuen Zeitalters, in dem neue Technologien – allen voran die Künstliche Intelligenz – völlig neue Möglichkeiten eröffnen. Für den Industriestandort Deutschland ist die Integration von KI in industrielle Prozesse eine enorme Chance auf dem Weg zu mehr Wettbewerbsfähigkeit. 

Der Übergang ins KI-Zeitalter ist mehr als nur eine technologische Evolution. KI wird die Arbeitswelt entscheidend verändern und neue Fähigkeiten fordern und fördern. Wir müssen dafür bei Bildung und Arbeit bestehende Muster durchbrechen und neue Wege gehen. Es gilt, die Menschen darauf vorzubereiten – angefangen bei der schulischen Ausbildung bis zu lebenslangem Lernen im beruflichen Umfeld und der Integration von KI in Arbeitsprozesse.

Als ein global führendes Unternehmen und einer der größten Arbeitgeber in Deutschland, sehen wir uns als Vordenker im Umgang mit KI. Wir ermutigen unsere Mitarbeitenden, ihre Kompetenzen ins KI-Zeitalter zu überführen, mit den neuen Technologien zu wachsen und diese mitzugestalten. Gleichzeitig legen wir in unserer Aus- und Weiterbildung Wert auf die Vermittlung grundlegender Fähigkeiten, wie etwa kritisches Denken, die Kernvoraussetzung für Entscheidungsfindung, Problemlösung und die Beurteilung von Informationen. Mit diesem umfassenden Skills-Ansatz sehen wir unsere Mitarbeitenden gut vorbereitet, um auch in Zeiten großer Technologieveränderungen für den Arbeitsmarkt langfristig relevant bleiben zu können.

KI ist da. Jetzt muss sie wirken. 
 
Die Ergebnisse aus unserer Mitarbeitenden-Befragung zeigen: Die regelmäßige KI-Nutzung bei der Deutschen Telekom ist erneut gestiegen – auf 83 Prozent. 

Das ist ein starkes Signal. Und es freut mich sehr.  

Denn KI entfaltet ihren Wert nicht dadurch, dass KI-Tools verfügbar ist. Entscheidend ist, dass Mitarbeitende die KI auch nutzen. Und – noch wichtiger – dass wir echte Wirkung damit erzielen. Deshalb bringen wir jetzt Struktur rein. Klar, unsere Leute bekommen die passenden Tools an die Hand. Und die bauen wir systematisch in Arbeitsprozesse ein:  

➡️ Unsere T-Cars planen die Glasfasertrassen automatisiert – mit KI und moderner Sensorik. 
➡️ Bei T-Systems arbeiten bereits rund 4.000 Software-Ingenieure mit unserem AI Engineer. 
➡️ Mit "Nadia" machen wir KI-gestütztes Coaching für Führungskräfte skalierbar. 
 
Genauso wichtig ist: Wir nehmen unsere Kolleginnen und Kollegen mit. Mit AI Explorer Journeys, Creatathons und AI Wizards, die Teams in Sachen KI beraten, schaffen wir Räume zum Lernen und Anwenden. Nicht jede und jeder muss KI-Expertin oder AI-Engineer werden. Was wir brauchen, sind Menschen, die ihr Fachwissen mit KI verbinden können und gleichzeitig ihre Urteilsfähigkeit bewahren. 

Mehr Nutzung ist gut. Aber der eigentliche Maßstab ist Wirkung: Verbessern wir Qualität und Service für unsere Kunden? Macht KI unsere Arbeit einfacher? Werden wir schneller? Schaffen wir Freiraum für die Dinge, die wirklich zählen?  

Und: KI ist nicht automatisch immer die beste Antwort. Unsere Kundinnen und Kunden wissen es zum Beispiel oft zu schätzen, dass sie in der Hotline oder im Shop mit einem echten Menschen sprechen können. 

Die steigende Nutzung an den richtigen Stellen ist ein wichtiger Schritt. Jetzt machen wir daraus echten Impact.

Bringing Top Leaders Back to School.

For three days in Munich, more than 200 Telekom leaders went back to school. To “AI School” 😊

Yesterday, we sat at our laptops, learned AI tools, tested them, challenged them, and built our own use cases. Today, we went even further: working concretely on rewiring work – changing workflows, roles, rules, and decision processes. 

AI creates so much more value when leaders move from talking about it to actually working with it.

That is what our T3 summit was about. The Telekom Transformation Team came together not because AI is new to us: AI is already part of our strategy and part of how we think about Performance, Uncorporate, and Collaboration.

What mattered now was the next step: building a shared leadership approach, setting the tone from the top, and doing it in a truly hands-on way.

Here are the convictions that I shared at our T3 summit. I believe they matter most to us now:

1️⃣ Huge AI promises still need fulfilling.
Adoption is high. Theoretical potential is huge. And we already see impressive use cases in our networks, in service, and in software engineering. But broad productivity effects are still limited. Why? Because tools alone do not transform companies. Work has to change.
 So the leadership task is clear: Don’t just add AI on top. Rewire work. 
 
2️⃣ Work will be re-imagined. Corporations will be re-designed.
AI will reshape roles, teams, and operating models. As leaders, we will need to lead and design hybrid teams – and some day we’ll ask: how is the Engagement score of the AI agents in your team? 😉
 
3️⃣ The winning combination is human experience and AI capability.
We have a strong culture and strong people. They truly make a difference. So the point is not human vs. machine. What counts is human experience, joy, intuition, courage, empathy. Amplified by AI.
Which also means: make conscious decisions. Be deliberate about what should be human-led, AI-supported, or AI-driven. And do not confuse fluent AI output with good judgment.
 
4️⃣ We need to address the social impact of AI.
AI raises real questions, for example around entry-level jobs.
Even if we cannot solve this alone, we cannot ignore it either. 
We need to act with responsibility. And we need to give orientation and involve our teams. People do not need perfect answers, but we shouldn’t leave them alone with uncertainty. 

And one more thing I take from Munich: Learn & and have fun with it. 😉
We learned a lot. We worked a lot. And we laughed a lot. 😊 (And that matters, too)

I’m optimistic: We have the tools. We have the openness. We have the learning.
Now we need to turn that into impact: From AI usage to AI impact.
Let’s do it T-Style.

A big shoutout to Nicole Hörl Muñoz & team, Jonathan Abrahamson, Peter Lorenz, Maximilian Ahrens for making this T3 summit happen!

Ich war noch ein Kind, als meine Mutter für drei Wochen durch den Himalaya reiste – und mich bei meinen Großeltern ließ. Ohne Drama, ohne schlechtes Gewissen, ohne Handy. Heute zum Weltfrauentag denke ich an diese Frau, die mich geprägt hat wie keine zweite: meine Mutter. Als Erste in der Familie machte sie Abitur, studierte, wurde Lehrerin. Sie war alleinerziehend – zu einer Zeit, in der das noch weniger Unterstützung und mehr Vorurteile bedeutete als heute. Und sie hat sich davon nicht definieren lassen. 

Was mich bis heute besonders beeindruckt: Sie hat sich nicht zwischen „Mutter sein“ und „arbeiten“ aufreiben lassen. Sie hat Verantwortung übernommen – für mich, für ihren Beruf als Lehrerin, in der Kirche, für Menschen im Hospiz, für Freunde. Aber sie hat sich eben auch immer wieder für sich selber Raum genommen. Für Dinge, die ihr Freude machen wie Reisen.
 
Am Weltfrauentag geht es aber nicht nur um persönliche Geschichten – sondern auch um Chancengerechtigkeit. Genau hier tragen wir auch als Arbeitgeber Verantwortung und bei der Deutschen Telekom stellen wir uns dieser Verantwortung. 
 
Ich darf an dieser Stelle heute einmal schreiben: Danke, Mama. Für deinen Mut. Für deine Freiheit. Für dein Lachen. Für deine klare Haltung und starken Werte. Für die Wurzeln und die Flügel, die Du mir mit auf den Weg gegeben hast.

To me, culture is like gardening.
 
A beautiful garden does not stay the same on its own. If you do not shape it, if you do not nourish or water it, it will stop flourishing. And whenever the weather, the seasons or even the climate is changing, the garden needs special care.
 
The same is true for company culture. We at Deutsche Telekom have a good culture. We have strong values. Our people are proud to be T. They feel they belong. They are engaged. 
But the world around us is changing. Stronger competition. Geopolitical uncertainty. A vibe shift in society.

That is why we decided to evolve our culture at Telekom. And we gave it a new name: T-Style.
 
At today’s Town Hall with Tim Höttges, I explained that gardening is never finished. And we are all gardeners. 
 
As Group, we are defining the frame. We have sharpened our Guiding principles and introduced our three cultural priorities: Performance, Uncorporate, Collaboration. 

However, culture can't be prescribed top-down. As top leaders we can inspire, we have to set the right conditions, we must walk the talk. 
But ultimately, culture is shaped by each and every colleague. By our individual decisions. By the way we work with one another. By the everyday actions we take.

That is why I shared a couple of examples at Telekom. Small, everyday examples that bring T-Style to life:

➡️ Our strong values: More than 100 colleagues donated blood this week here in Bonn – organized by our trainees. A strong example of solidarity and responsibility for the greater good. This is T-Style!
➡️ Collaboration: Our new intranet is being built by a team collaborating across many functions. And more than 10.000 colleagues have already voted for a name. This is what collaboration looks like in practice. Or if my colleagues Rodrigo Diehl and Dr. Ferri Abolhassan drop fire-up messages to me before and during the townhall. This is T-Style!
➡️ The Uncorporate: In my own leadership team, we are testing a simple principle: No decision to make? No meeting. And more time for what really matters. This is T-Style!
➡️ Performance: Whether it is frontline technicians striving for "excellent craftsmanship" for our customers, or colleagues like Ulrich Klenke going the extra mile to make a video truly excellent: this is ambition, devotion and performance in action. This is T-Style!
 
And there were many more great examples today: colleagues and teams who presented projects that truly bring T-Style to life. These projects really deserve the T-Style stamp of excellence! Thank you for sharing your work and your energy.

Ash Wednesday in the Rhineland means one thing: Carnival is over, the costumes are gone – and it’s time for clarity. 

At our oneHR Kick-off, we talked about what we need to deliver in 2026 - and even more about HOW we will deliver it.

We started off with a reflection on the past year. 2025 was not an “easy year” – and still, the HR colleagues at Deutsche Telekom delivered. Big transformations, real progress on skills, our values stayed strong even under pressure, and yes: well-deserved awards across countries and teams. Congrats and thank you to everyone who made that happen!  

Looking ahead, our Culture 2.0 will guide us in 2026 and beyond. 
We call it T-Style. And it consists of: 

➡️Our Group Purpose: We won’t stop until everyone is connected 
➡️Our strong values, our Guiding Principles 
➡️Clear cultural priorities: Performance, the Uncorporate, Collaboration 
➡️And the spirit we want to bring into 2026: optimism.  
 
And our HR priorities we set ourselves for 2026 will be powered by T-Style: 
 
1️⃣  We’ll drive and support transformation: We will keep adapting our organization to what the business needs – responsibly and with our social partners. It’s about doing the hard work thoughtfully, with people in mind.

2️⃣ We want to move from AI usage to impact. Tools are everywhere and more than 75% of our people already use them. But real impact only comes when workflows change. Therefore, we are investing more in our AI enablement, our internal chatbot AskT, as well as in our growth hub platform as a global lever for skills and development.  

3️⃣  We keep our colleagues’ engagement high – and turn insights into measures. Transformation needs energy, pride, and belonging. Therefore, we are introducing a shared engagement metric across all segments. 

4️⃣  We are growing our leaders – more diverse, ready to shape the future. The bar is rising, and we are investing into our talent programs and future skills.

5️⃣  On HR data and IT, we’ll build the foundation and raise the experience for our colleagues. What we’ll work on further: Simplifying heavy processes, improving service quality, clean data and stable systems, and one employee “front door”. 
 
A big thank you to my HR Leadership Team for driving this agenda – and for presenting T-Style today with so much conviction. And THANK YOU to all involved in making this oneHR Kick-off happen!  
 
I said it to my team today, and I’ll keep repeating it:  
Be leading. Be T-Style.

Be leading. Be T-Style.
 
Telekom’s company culture is strong. Our values are well-anchored and our purpose guides us: We won’t stop until everyone is connected.
 
But the world does not stand still. Competition is getting fierce, more and more. We feel a vibe shift: values that once felt widely shared are coming under pressure. And geopolitics is changing the rules of the game. 
 
In this environment, we as Deutsche Telekom are now evolving our culture.
 
We call it: T-Style
 
And today, at our annual Telekom Top Management Team Meeting – #TMTM, I showed what this means for us as leaders. 
 
We are building on the strong foundation of our Guiding Principles. We sharpen them now. To reflect what the moment requires: embracing technology, scaling globally, and the need to be leading. 
 
And we are setting three priorities. They will be our focus areas for 2026 and the years to come:
 
▪️ Performance: Sometimes we shy away from honest, critical conversations about underperformance – and we don’t always recognize high performance strongly enough. It’s clear to us: We have to raise the bar before the market raises it for us.
▪️ The Uncorporate: We complain about bureaucracy a lot when it comes to government agencies. But now it’s on us to act: We’ll challenge our own internal processes, IT systems, and hierarchies. We’ll remove the clutter and make room for ideas and innovation.
▪️ Collaboration: It is often strong within teams already. Now we need even more of it across teams, segments, and countries. Because we win as a network, not as silos.
 
And we already have many examples where we are T-Style today:
▪️ Our teams in networks and services, winning award after award.
▪️ Teams responding in moments that matter – like a power outage in Berlin or supporting communities during floods in Poland.
▪️ The team that brought the Industrial AI Cloud to life, offering data sovereignty in Germany
▪️ Thousands of colleagues giving their time for “Ein Herz für Kinder.”
 
These examples underline what our CEO Tim Höttges said today: culture is not “HR stuff”. Culture is business. It creates value. And it is what differentiates us.
 
From now on, when we as Telekom are at our very best, we will say: “This is T-Style.”
And it’s up to each and every one of us to live this T-Style .
 
That’s why I told my colleagues today, and I will keep saying it across Telekom:
 
Be leading. Be T-Style.

KI mit Zuversicht. 🤝
 
In vielen Gesprächen und in meinen Roundtables mit Mitarbeitenden bekomme ich sehr konkrete Fragen zum Thema Künstliche Intelligenz:
 
👉 Wird es meinen Job in ein paar Jahren noch geben?
👉 Wie kann ich Experte werden, wenn Einstiegsaufgaben wegfallen?
👉 Wie verändert KI unsere Zusammenarbeit?
 
Ehrlich: Für manches haben wir noch keine endgültigen Antworten. Aber ich bin voller Zuversicht. Aus drei Gründen: 
 
1️⃣ KI ist im Arbeitsalltag angekommen.
In unserer aktuellen Mitarbeitendenbefragung sagen 53 % der Mitarbeitenden, dass sie KI regelmäßig in ihrer Arbeit nutzen. Das sind 9 Prozentpunkte mehr als noch vor einem halben Jahr. Ein weiteres Viertel (24%) nutzt KI schon ab und an. 
Ob im Vertrieb, in der Technik, beim Coden oder mit unserem Assistenten askT, der jeden Monat hunderttausende Fragen beantwortet: KI macht Arbeit einfacher, besser und effizienter.
 
2️⃣ Wir investieren ins Lernen.
Über 100.000 Mitarbeitende haben schon an KI-Trainings teilgenommen. Unsere AI Explorer Journeys & AI Promptathons wurden gerade mit dem HR Excellence Award ausgezeichnet. Gratulation ans Team! 
Das ist ein starkes Signal: Unsere Leute wollen lernen. Und sie tun es. 
 
3️⃣ Was mir am meisten Zuversicht gibt: KI ist nicht von oben verordnet.
Ich freue mich immer besonders, wenn die Initiative von unseren Mitarbeitenden ausgeht. Zum Beispiel beim ExplorAItion Day. Da teilen Kolleginnen und Kollegen ihre eigenen KI-Anwendungsfälle, lernen voneinander und probieren neue KI-Ideen aus. Über 1.600 Mitarbeitende waren Mitte November dabei.
So leben wir KI bei der Telekom: mit Neugierde und Einfach machen!
 
Bei der Telekom ist KI kein Widerspruch zu guter Arbeit, sondern ein Werkzeug, um sie weiterzuentwickeln. Mit dem Menschen im Mittelpunkt.

4️⃣ Künstliche Intelligenz leistet ihren Beitrag zu Guter Arbeit. Unser Chatbot AskT hat schon über drei Millionen Gespräche mit Mitarbeitenden geführt. Dass wir mit den Betriebsräten und ver.di an Guter Arbeit gemeinsam arbeiten, dafür bin ich dankbar. Genauso dafür, dass sie die #Sozialpartnerschaft mitgestalten. Mit Engagement, Streitlust, Geduld und Realitätssinn 😉.

Living Culture Day: Doing Good Makes Us Stronger
 
Today, it’s Living Culture Day: Here in Bonn and all over the world, Deutsche Telekom is celebrating our values and the “Power of We”. Today’s motto was “Together for Good”. It is so great to have many colleagues around the world in our company actively engaged in good causes, like: 
🩷 Our efforts during natural disasters like the floods in Valencia and Ahr Valley or the wildfires in Greece. 
🩷 Our fundraising campaigns to support people in need—for example, in Poland and India. 
🩷 Our committed involvement, e.g. with the Special Olympics, Ein Herz für Kinder, and Germany’s Relief Coalition. 
🩷 Our engagement for our Telekom communities like Magenta Pride, the Neurodiversity Community or for Digital@School. 

Our commitment not only helps others but also strengthens us as colleagues and teams. Enabling us to act even better for our customers and to contribute to our business.

ZuMUTung + ZuverSICHT = Zukunft
 
Das ist heute meine Botschaft an die Leitenden Angestellten der Deutschen Telekom gewesen. 
 
Was ich damit meine? 
 
Führung heißt gerade jetzt: Wir brauchen Klartext und einen klaren Blick fürs Business. Stagnierende Wirtschaft, ein perfect storm in einigen Branchen, hohe Personalnebenkosten. Das bedeutet, gerade am Standort Deutschland wird es Zukunft ohne Zumutungen nicht geben.
 
In „Zumutung“ steckt aber auch Mut. Mut, Dinge anders zu machen. Indem jede und jeder Einzelne über sich hinauswächst. Wenn wir das schaffen, dann sind wir nicht nur Getriebene der Zumutung. Sondern dann können wir Zumutung aktiv in Fortschritt drehen. 
 
Da beginnt für mich Zuversicht. 
 
Zuversicht nicht als „Prinzip Hoffnung“, sondern als Richtung, als klare Sicht. Die haben wir als Telekom – strategisch, kulturell, technologisch:
•	Unser Strategie-Flywheel dreht sich, mit globaler Skalierung und Daten & KI als Hebel. 
•	Unser Wertefundament steht. Selbst wenn das Umfeld schwieriger wird, unsere Kultur stärken wir. 
•	KI ist bei unseren Mitarbeitenden angekommen. Mehr als 100.000 absolvierte Trainings im Konzern – das macht mich zuversichtlich! Und mit unserem growth hub werden wir die eine globale Plattform für alle Mitarbeitenden schaffen, die Skills, Entwicklungsmöglichkeiten und Chancen zusammenbringt. 
 
Zumutungen und Zuversicht – beides ergibt Zukunft. Sie zu gestalten, das ist unsere Aufgabe als Führungskräfte. 

Oder wie es mein Vorstandskollege Rodrigo Diehl ausgedrückt hat: Mich motiviert eine Krise auch, weil daraus immer eine Chance entstehen kann. Das chinesische Schriftzeichen für Krise besteht aus den zwei einzelnen Zeichen für Gefahr und Möglichkeit. Es ist an uns Führungskräften, die Gefahr zu managen und die Chance zu ergreifen. 

Danke an Roland Angst und das Team für die starke Veranstaltung. Und Reminder: Nächstes Jahr sind die Wahlen zum Konzernsprecherausschuss, also die Vertretung der leitenden Angestellten. Gelebte Demokratie im Unternehmen. Vielen Dank an alle, die sich zur Wahl stellen und sich engagieren.

When I met Zsuzsanna for the first time in 2019, she told me that it was her aspiration to once be a legend in HR. And already then I was impressed. Today I have the privilege to have her in my team. And I can tell that this award is well deserved 🎉🍾💃🏼

„Ich bin Jolanda, meine Pronomen sind sie/ihr“ – was für manche ein Stolperstein ist, ist für Jolanda Gallas Alltag und ein Statement. Denn wer mit ihr spricht, merkt schnell: Es geht ihr nicht nur um Sichtbarkeit, sondern um echte Veränderung.

Als Spokesperson der Community MagentaPride im Ehrenamt und Sustainability Consultant bei der Telekom MMS im Hauptjob, verbindet Jolanda Überzeugung mit Verantwortung. Seit neun Jahren ist sie im Konzern, seit drei Jahren bei MagentaPride aktiv. Die Community gibt es bereits seit 2001, um sich im Arbeitskontext gegen Diskriminierung aufgrund der sexuellen Orientierung gegenseitig zu unterstützen. Heute engagieren sich rund 40 queere Mitarbeitende im Kernteam von MagentaPride. Zusätzlich bringen sich zahlreiche Allies, also unterstützende Kolleg*innen unabhängig von ihrer eigenen Identität, für Themen wie Awareness, Sensibilisierung und gelebte Vielfalt ein. Auf Instagram folgen der Community sogar über 1.500 Menschen. Ziel ist es, ein inklusives Umfeld zu schaffen, in dem niemand die eigene Identität ‚am Eingang zum Büro‘ abgeben muss – denn wer ganz man selbst sein kann, muss keine Energie ins Verstellen stecken und kann sich auf das konzentrieren, worum es wirklich geht: die Arbeit.

Jolanda weiß: Das Thema queere Sichtbarkeit ist aktueller denn je. Physische und psychische Gewalt an queeren Personen hat sich seit 2010 verzehnfacht, „über 20 Prozent der Gen Z identifizieren sich als queer“. Für sie ein Zeichen, wie wichtig es ist, offen und sensibel mit Vielfalt umzugehen. Dennoch seien viele Menschen unsicher, weil sie Angst haben, etwas falsch zu machen, sagt Jolanda. „Aber es ist besser, offen nachzufragen, als zu schweigen.“ 

Für die 27-Jährige ist ihr Engagement auch persönlich. Sie ist selbst queer und hat sich erst nach dem Studium geoutet. Ein Prozess, der Mut und Vorbilder erforderte. Heute möchte sie selbst ein solches Vorbild sein. Schon in der Schule war sie Schülersprecherin, mit einem ausgeprägten Gerechtigkeitssinn. Jetzt kämpft sie dafür, dass sich niemand im Job verstellen muss – ganz gleich, welche Identität oder Orientierung man hat. Und es gibt Fortschritte: Sensibilisierungstrainings, Netzwerktreffen für Nachwuchskräfte, eine stärkere Präsenz auf Events wie dem CSD, eine Parade und Demonstration für die Rechte von LGBTQIA+-Menschen und eine internationale MagentaPride Community. 
Das Team arbeitet daran, noch sichtbarer und zugänglicher zu werden – auch in Zusammenarbeit mit anderen Diversity-Communities im Unternehmen. Denn: „Alle Menschen sind bunt – nicht nur queer, sondern auch in Herkunft, Fähigkeiten, Perspektiven.“

Jolandas Wunschbild für die Zukunft? Eine Telekom, in der queere Identitäten ganz selbstverständlich dazugehören. Und doch will sie nicht, dass MagentaPride eines Tages überflüssig wird: „Die Community bietet so viel wertvollen Austausch – sie ist ein Ort der Verbindung, nicht nur der Sichtbarkeit.“
