📊 Understanding the Balance Sheet: A Snapshot of a Company's Financial Health

One of the most important financial statements every finance student and professional should understand is the Balance Sheet.

A balance sheet provides a snapshot of what a company owns (Assets), owes (Liabilities), and the owner's share (Equity) at a specific point in time.

Here's a simple way to understand it:

✅ Assets – Resources owned by the company, such as cash, inventory, buildings, and equipment.

✅ Liabilities – Financial obligations the company needs to pay, such as loans, creditors, and outstanding expenses.

✅ Owner's Equity – The owner's investment in the business after deducting liabilities from assets.

The basic accounting equation is:

Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity

Why is a Balance Sheet important?

📌 It helps assess a company's financial position.
📌 It supports investment and lending decisions.
📌 It shows how efficiently a company manages its resources.
📌 It is one of the key financial statements used by managers, investors, and analysts.

As an MBA Finance graduate, I believe understanding financial statements is the foundation of making informed business decisions.

🚨 Common Resume Mistakes You Should Avoid

A strong resume does more than list your experience—it should quickly show employers why you're a great fit for the role. 📄✨

Here are 6 common mistakes that can reduce the impact of your resume:

❌ 1. Using a Generic Resume
🎯 Tailor your resume to the specific position and employer instead of sending the same version everywhere.

❌ 2. Writing a Weak Profile Summary
📝 Your opening summary should clearly communicate your experience, strengths, and career value.

❌ 3. Listing Responsibilities Without Achievements
🏆 Don't just say what you were responsible for. Highlight results, improvements, and measurable accomplishments.

❌ 4. Poor Formatting and Too Much Text
📋 Keep your resume clean, structured, and easy to scan. Recruiters often review resumes quickly.

❌ 5. Missing Job-Specific Keywords
🔑 Use relevant skills and keywords from the job description—especially important when resumes are screened by ATS systems.

❌ 6. Grammar, Spelling, and Formatting Errors
✅ Small mistakes can make a resume look careless. Always proofread before submitting.

💡 Remember: Your resume should be easy to read, relevant to the role, and focused on achievements—not just duties.

👉 Before applying for your next job, take a few minutes to review your resume against these six points.

Inversión extranjera directa: una inyección de confianza para la economía dominicana

La República Dominicana continúa consolidándose como uno de los destinos más atractivos para la inversión en América Latina y el Caribe. El crecimiento sostenido de la Inversión Extranjera Directa (IED) refleja algo más que la entrada de capitales: representa confianza en la estabilidad económica, el potencial productivo y las oportunidades de desarrollo que ofrece el país.

Detrás de cada inversión existen nuevas empresas, expansión de operaciones, generación de empleos, transferencia de conocimientos y oportunidades para fortalecer sectores estratégicos. Turismo, zonas francas, energía, tecnología, logística, manufactura y bienes raíces figuran entre las áreas que continúan captando el interés de inversionistas internacionales.

Este dinamismo también plantea importantes desafíos. El crecimiento de la inversión debe traducirse en mayor productividad, empleos de calidad, desarrollo regional y encadenamientos con las pequeñas y medianas empresas locales. La meta no debe limitarse a atraer más capital, sino a lograr que ese capital genere un impacto sostenible y ampliamente distribuido.

Para mantener esta trayectoria, será fundamental continuar fortaleciendo la seguridad jurídica, la transparencia institucional, la formación del talento humano y la infraestructura. Un entorno competitivo y predecible permite que la inversión no solo llegue, sino que permanezca, se expanda y contribuya al crecimiento de largo plazo.

La inversión extranjera directa es una señal clara de confianza, pero también una oportunidad estratégica. El reto para la República Dominicana consiste en convertir ese flujo de capital en innovación, competitividad y bienestar para más ciudadanos.

El crecimiento de la inversión es una buena noticia. Transformarla en desarrollo sostenible será la verdadera medida del éxito.

After a 40-year career in HR—and over five truly incredible years at Google —I have decided to retire at the end of Q2. My family all lives in Europe, and as my mum gets older, I want to prioritize spending quality time with them.

While I’m sharing this news externally today, this transition has been thoughtfully underway for several months. I recently first shared my plans internally at Google and with my People Operations organization back in March, and will be staying on for a short period to support the team’s transition. The company expects to name a new Chief People Officer sometime later this year.

When I look back over the last four decades, it is astonishing to see how much the HR profession has evolved. We've gone through periods where the function was heavily weighed down by process and administration, but today, we are on the cusp of something extraordinary.

Watching AI begin to fundamentally reshape how we work fills me with so much hope and excitement for the future of HR. Is it finally going to strip away the process work and allow teams to do what they do best: focus entirely on the human element? I truly hope so.

I’m so grateful to have worked with many amazing companies and my time at Google has undoubtedly been the highlight of my career. Leading this team and seeing the company transform through our hard work and change management has been the privilege of my life. Google is a remarkably special place, full of kind and brilliant people who are actively building the future and shaping the world as we lean into the age of AI.

Professionally, it is difficult to step away when things are this exciting, but personal and professional timelines rarely align perfectly. I am so proud of what the People Operations team has built together to set the foundations for this success—supporting Google and Googlers to get ready for this new era.

As I prepare to pass the baton, I want to send a massive, heartfelt thank you to my colleagues, mentors, friends and family who have made this journey what it was. I will be cheering you all on from the sidelines forever! 🥰

Rahul Jindal's latest paper on “Organizational Metabolism” is a masterclass in shifting our focus from AI adoption to AI absorption. His core thesis? The real differentiator in 2026 isn't your technology budget—it’s your "Metabolic Rate."
The framework’s biggest win is the concept of Workflow Debt. We are often layering AI on top of legacy processes instead of retiring them. As Rahul puts it: "Low-metabolism organizations accumulate experiments. High-metabolism organizations retire workflows."
The one piece I think we still need to solve for: The Emotional Metabolism.
While the structural roadmap is brilliant, we can’t ignore the "human immune system." Retiring a workflow can feel like retiring an identity. I can't quite believe it's already been five years since I joined Google, it feels like I joined just 5 days ago, it's gone so quickly.

I was wowed by the people and excited to see Google’s innovative workplace in action. I knew it would be brilliant. I knew it would move fast and I was ready to go. We were right in the middle of Covid, and I remember straining to pick up the cultural nuances through a video (that was hard!).

Still, I could never have imagined the dizzying pace of innovation or the scale of technological progress we’ve seen these past few years. AI is transforming everything—from how we fight fires and treat cancer, to how we travel and get work done. It feels like every week we’re making huge leaps forward in computing, in our models, and in how we apply them for the benefit of our users and the world.

Yesterday, I had the honor of moderating an incredibly inspiring World Economic Forum session on AI and the future of work, with two visionary leaders Judson Althoff and Carl Eschenbach. Yesterday’s discussion made it clear that while AI continues to transform our world, it is our people – with their creativity, adaptability, and judgment – who are powering the future. 

We came away with three clear lessons leaders can use when empowering people to lead with AI:

1. Optimism over anxiety. The conversation is shifting, and employees are increasingly hopeful about what AI can do for them and their organizations. Success starts with leaders who champion and empower their teams to see challenges as opportunities. 

2. AI is for everyone. Universal adoption is key. AI should amplify every employee’s impact, regardless of their role. Commit to championing AI literacy in your organization, ensuring every person has the confidence and skills to thrive alongside AI tools. 

3. AI is the tool, but people are the power. Your people are the engine of transformation – fuel them. As leaders, we must invest in both cutting-edge tools and world-class training equally. When we do both, we do more than adopt AI – we lead the future.

Thank you to Judson and Carl for sharing your perspectives in such an insightful discussion. I look forward to helping shape the future of work we discussed – a future where AI amplifies and empowers what makes us uniquely human. #WEF26 Workday Microsoft

Today marks #WorldCancerDay, a day that hits close to home for me.

Cancer has affected my life in very personal ways—my dad fought prostate cancer for more than 17 years and my mom faced stage 3b breast cancer. And just last year, one of my routine screenings came back with an irregular result. Like so many people who face this type of unexpected news during their preventive screenings, my first reaction was fear. Thanks to Merck’s comprehensive benefits, I was able to quickly get follow-up testing and a biopsy — and fortunately, everything came back clear.

These tough moments remind me of how much access and support matter. That’s why I am so proud of the progress our company has made in support of cancer prevention and early detection. In under a year, we have expanded access to WHO-recommended screenings (breast, cervical, colorectal), HPV-related cancer vaccinations, and the time and flexibility to use these services—now reaching more than 96% of employees and their families across 71 countries. The team continues the hard work to extend these benefits where they are not yet available.  

I’m so grateful to everyone at Merck who made this possible and to all those working tirelessly to advance cancer prevention, early detection and care.

Transformation is no longer a sequence of initiatives – it is happening everywhere, all at once.

At the German-speaking SAP User Group (DSAG e.V.) Personaltage event in Heidelberg, discussions showed: the shift toward an #AutonomousEnterprise is not about automation in the traditional sense. It is about intelligent assistants and agents that can operate end-to-end; augmented, orchestrated, and always with humans in the loop.

Three core takeaways I shared with the audience:
➖ Rewiring the organization for an AI-native world
We are moving from vertical silos to horizontal, end-to-end value streams. Agents operate across domains, so organizations must follow. This requires new operating models, orchestration layers, and hybrid teams where humans and AI collaborate seamlessly.
➖ Skills as the foundation of adaptability
With skill half-lives shrinking to 6–18 months, organizations need to become truly skill-based. “Learn to unlearn,” continuous reskilling, and real-time skill intelligence are becoming core capabilities for staying relevant.
➖ Human leadership remains central
In an Autonomous Enterprise, humans stay in the driver’s seat. Judgment, empathy, and ethical guardrails matter more, not less. The real challenge is to create the conditions for people to adopt, trust, and effectively work with AI.
 
During our joint panel, Hermann-Josef Haag, Board Member at DSAG, moderator Juliane Krampe, and I debated the following:
➖ Transformation is less a technology challenge, but increasingly a people, prioritization, and leadership challenge
➖ Organizations are managing multiple shifts at once: AI, architecture changes, workforce transformation, and external pressures
➖ The biggest pain points we see across customers are strategic workforce planning, skills transparency, and connecting data across HR, finance, and processes
➖ Progress requires clear target states and pragmatic, phased execution
➖ And most importantly: no organization can navigate this alone. Ecosystems and exchange are critical
 
From a broader SAP perspective, this reinforces our direction: enabling customers to run end-to-end business processes with integrated AI, data, and applications, while embedding people, skills, and change deeply into our transformation journey. Because ultimately, becoming an Autonomous Enterprise is about building adaptive organizations and ensuring employees have the enablement, support, and confidence to thrive in this new reality.

The pace will not slow down. The differentiator will be how deliberately we combine technology and human potential to shape what comes next.

AI transformation becomes real only when people, business, and ecosystem move together.
 
That became very tangible for me last week across Singapore, Melbourne, and Sydney. I had the opportunity to speak and engage with customers, partners, employees, and early-career talent, and the core questions were remarkably consistent: How do we turn AI ambition into adoption? How do we redesign work, not just add tools? And how do we build the skills and leadership needed to make that transition real?

My conversations with customers and partners made one thing very clear: people strategy is business strategy. In CHRO roundtables, customer meetings, and partner exchanges, the focus was not only on technology, but on workforce transformation, skills, AI adoption, and performance culture. That is exactly where our People Agenda becomes a business agenda. 
The same was true in our global People & Culture Employee Meeting live from Singapore. One reason I valued the session with Alexandra Steiger so much is that it reinforced the outside-in perspective: strategy is important, but the real question is how credibly we translate it into organizational readiness, workforce capability, and measurable progress.

During last week’s HANNOVER MESSE, one thing became very clear: AI is already embedded in real business processes – from the shop floor to supply chains and enterprise systems.
At the SAP booth, this became tangible through a simple but powerful example: the production of a ginger shot. From planning and mixing to packaging and delivery, AI connects the entire process – with agents monitoring production, robots inspecting quality, and AI copilots supporting decisions in real time. What used to be fragmented becomes one integrated flow.
 
This is a remarkable shift: AI is not just supporting tasks. It is orchestrating outcomes across systems, teams, and physical operations. A simple way to think about it: It’s Monday morning. You start your job – and your AI teammate is already at work. Analyzing data, simulating scenarios, preparing decisions. What changes is not just speed. What changes is how work itself is designed.
 
But technology alone does not create value. The real question is whether we are redesigning work fast enough to unlock its full potential.
Because this transformation changes the fundamentals: We go from executing tasks to orchestrating outcomes, from rigid roles to dynamic skills, and from isolated tools to integrated, AI-supported processes.
 
That was the focus of our engaging discussion on the Center Stage: Skills are becoming the new currency of work. In a world where capabilities evolve continuously, the differentiator is not what people know today, but how quickly they learn, adapt, and apply.
 
For companies, this means: AI transformation is not a technology program. It is a work redesign and leadership challenge. Technology creates potential, but organizations need to learn how to turn it into impact.

That dip exists because work is being rebuilt while results are not yet visible. People are learning new skills, roles are shifting, and processes are being redesigned at the same time. The critical mistake is to interpret this phase as failure. In reality, it’s where the real work happens – rebuilding skills, processes, and ways of working.

The hardest part of AI transformation is not the technology. It is changing how work actually gets done.

Research points in the same direction: only a small share of AI value comes from the algorithms themselves. The bigger shift happens through people, processes and leadership; when organizations rethink roles, build new skills, and redesign how work happens.
That was at the heart of our first People & Culture Manager Day and the 2026 P&C Kick-Off at SAP, where colleagues from Mannheim, Prague, Bangalore, Newtown Square, Manila and many other locations came together to discuss what this means for the business and for P&C in particular.

Several insights stood out for me:
➔ Futurrist Ian Beacraft challenged us to think beyond automation: AI is reshaping how work is designed, how decisions are made, and which human capabilities create the most value.
➔ Kathi Enderes reinforced that the biggest barriers to AI impact are rarely technical, but organizational: skills, leadership, and the ability to translate technology into new ways of working.
➔ And in our panel with Pinar Dolen, Marielle Ehrmann, Dr. Magdalena Masluk-Meller Eric Goldstein and Ian, one point became very clear: if AI is reshaping the business, then People & Culture must transform too.

For us, that means three things in particular: rethinking how work happens with AI at the core, building new skills while unlearning outdated limits, and connecting more effectively across roles and teams to create impact faster.

For People & Culture, this is a defining moment. We’re not watching work change - we’re making it happen: redesigning the operating model, building the skills, and shaping the culture that turns AI into impact.

AI investments are at an all-time high. But a central question for leaders across industries is no longer whether to adopt AI. It’s how to build the capabilities to work with it.

Research gives us some insights on what matters most: Only 10% of AI value comes from algorithms, 20% from technology and data. But 70% comes from people, processes, and leadership. AI transformation is also a leadership and organizational transformational story, not just technology.

This perspective came alive this week at the Münchner Management Kolloquium at Technical University of Munich, where executives, scientists, and founders gathered under the theme “Bold Moves: Managing with Courage” to discuss how Europe can remain competitive in a rapidly changing technological landscape. In our panel with Britta Seeger, Bettina Dietsche, and Dane Molter, moderated by Prof. Dr. Claudia Peus, we explored how AI at work is crafting tomorrow.

One thing became clear: When technology evolves every few months, value no longer comes from what we know, but from how fast we adapt. That is why SAP is moving toward a skills‑led organization. We are entering a world where the shelf life of skills is shrinking dramatically, sometimes to just months.  
Therefore, the real challenge is not introducing AI. It is redesigning work, processes, operating models and skills at the speed AI evolves.

This year’s #MMK26 showed that we are ready for these bold moves. When companies, universities, and communities work together to prepare people for a world where humans and AI collaborate, we are not just ready for the future – we're actively designing it.

Thank you to Ricarda Engelmeier, Prof. Dr. Dr. h. c. mult. Horst Wildemann and everyone who contributed to such a thoughtful discussion.

We Win as One: Growing Together as a Global Team at SAP 

From Munich to Paris to Walldorf – the past two weeks have been an incredible opportunity to connect with so many SAP colleagues. I took the time to listen, exchange ideas, and bring home new perspectives and feedback that will shape my work as Chief People Officer. 

What stood out most to me was the energy, openness, and genuine commitment everyone brings to our shared goals. Every conversation reminded me how powerful it is when we come together as one team – to learn, challenge each other, and move forward together. 

We covered so many important topics – from integrating AI into our daily work and creating growth opportunities across generations, to making space for learning and keeping a people-first mindset at the heart of everything we do. I especially appreciated the honest discussions about what’s working well and where we can do better. Those candid moments are what help us grow. 

A highlight for me was discussing how to keep the human factor alive in the age of AI. One initiative I’m particularly proud of is our new People & Culture Lounges – now available in over 60 countries. Employees can schedule a more personal, local HR consultation with a colleague to address questions directly and benefit from in-depth, face-to-face conversations, helping them find the right support for both professional and personal growth. 

Across all locations, one thing became crystal clear: “We win as one” isn’t just one of our GROWTH Culture behaviors – it’s how we work. From the new collaboration-friendly offices in Garching, to open and critical discussions in Garching and Paris, to celebrating with our People & Culture community at our employee meeting in Walldorf, I’ve seen firsthand how connection, trust, and shared purpose help us reach our full potential. 

A heartfelt thank-you to everyone who joined, shared their thoughts, and made these moments so meaningful. I’m already looking forward to our next conversations and continuing this journey together.  

#PeopleAtSAP #Teamwork #FutureOfWork

Keeping the Human Factor in the age of AI at UNLEASH World Conference 2025 in Paris – What an inspiring day! 
  
At UNLEASH, a global HR community came together this week in Paris to discuss the power of people, technology and transformation. Connecting with the many brilliant minds from across the globe was one of my highlights and once again inspired me to lead the change at SAP. Starting off with a fireside chat with Bruce Daisley on how AI’s real power emerges when paired with human creativity and the importance of building workplaces where people not only perform – but flourish. We concluded that thriving in a tech-driven era means balancing innovative tools with nurturing people’s growth, agility, and sense of purpose. 
  
During the later CHRO Summit, the conversations went deep into how we can redesign roles, teams, and workflows to empower people and foster adaptive cultures. We had the pleasure of listening to a keynote by Josh Bersin who tied together the need for the right skills to redesign how work is done in the age of AI and stressed the importance of skills agility. Building on that, Isabelle Minneci and I shared insights on how CHROs can stay proactive by continuously reinventing HR strategies. Isabelle brought deep insights from her work at L’Oréal, and together we discussed how AI and humans together truly form a power couple, bringing together the best of two worlds. 
  
I also had the chance to discuss these themes on the HR Leaders Podcast with Christopher Rainey, diving into how SAP is leading a shift toward skills-first workforce strategies and leveraging AI thoughtfully to boost well-being and flexibility – a great wrap-up to both the event and my visit in Paris. Stay tuned for that episode. 
  
Thank you to the #UNLEASH team and everyone who joined!

Zukunft made in Germany: 300 Millionen Euro für Technologie. Bis zu 700 neue Jobs bis 2030.   

Das bedeutet für uns: Chancen für Menschen. Perspektiven für die Region. Investition in Zukunftsfähigkeit.    

Wir investieren 300 Millionen Euro in Frankfurt und Offenbach, um Schlüsseltechnologien auszubauen, die die globale #Energiewende vorantreiben und die wachsende Nachfrage nach Infrastruktur für #KI-Rechenzentren bedienen können. Bis 2030 entstehen dabei bis zu 700 neue Arbeitsplätze – in Fertigung, Logistik und Verwaltung.   

Diese Investition ist nicht nur eine Frage von Technologie und Infrastruktur. Vielmehr geht es darum, echte Perspektiven zu schaffen – für die Menschen in der Region und für den Standort Deutschland:  

👥 Chancen für Menschen – Wir qualifizieren unsere Mitarbeitenden kontinuierlich weiter, damit sie die Kompetenzen entwickeln können, die im KI-Zeitalter gefragt sind. Denn nachhaltige #Beschäftigungsfähigkeit entsteht durch lebenslanges Lernen.   

📍 Perspektiven für die Region – Mit künftig drei Werken in Frankfurt und Offenbach schaffen wir Arbeitsplätze für unterschiedlichste Qualifikationen und stärken damit eine der wirtschaftlich wichtigsten Regionen Deutschlands.   

🚀 Investition in Zukunftsfähigkeit – Bei Siemens investieren wir nicht nur in Technologie, sondern ermöglichen es Menschen, diese Technologie mit Leidenschaft sinnvoll einzusetzen. Das macht uns stark – und stärkt die Wettbewerbsfähigkeit des Standorts #Deutschland.   

Für mich ist diese Investition ein klares Signal: Deutschland bleibt ein starker Industrie- und Technologiestandort – wenn Menschen mit Können, Neugier und Verantwortung handeln. Genau das macht den Unterschied – heute und morgen. 💪

A symbiosis of nature, technology and the communities in the #Amazonia.

Speaking with Charmian (Char) Love from Natura at HANNOVER MESSE meant a lot to me. We have a shared passion - the #Moiru project is a joint initiative by Natura, Siemens, and a local community nested in the world’s most critical forest. 🌿🌳

Moiru means mutual support in Tupi, one of the many indigenous languages of the Amazonia. And it is everything this initiative stands for.

In the heart of the Amazonia, communities produce essential oils for Natura’s cosmetics - rooted in generations of knowledge and a deep connection with the forest.

With Siemens’ digital technology, the process of extraction has become safer, more stable and efficient - using less energy and water - and the outcome more reliable and better in quality.

This is what we mean by Technology with Purpose:
👉 Not replacing tradition, but building on it.
👉 Not taking from nature, but creating regenerative value locally.
👉 Not leaving people behind, but giving them the tools and agency to shape their own future and protect the land they love.

It is a great reminder on #EarthDay today: Businesses can be powerful forces for good - by building models that work with nature, and for people. 🌎

Die Bitkom #TRANSFORM26 in Berlin war für mich ein wertvoller Impulsgeber: Wenn es um Transformation geht, müssen Politik und Wirtschaft eng zusammenrücken.

Im Dialog mit Bundesministerin Karin Prien (BMBFSFJ) und Marcel Fratzscher, Leiter des DIW, stand die zentrale Frage im Raum: „Diversity, Equity, Irrelevance: Kann unsere Wirtschaft auf Vielfalt verzichten?“

Die Antwort ist klar: Gerade für die digitale Transformation und zur Sicherung unserer Wettbewerbsfähigkeit ist #Vielfalt unverzichtbar. Sie ist kein „Nice-to-have“, sondern – in all ihren Facetten – ein entscheidender Wettbewerbsvorteil und ein Motor für #Innovation. Mehr Vielfalt, auch und insbesondere durch mehr Frauen, ist für die Wirtschaft essenziell.

Und mit Blick auf die demografischen Veränderungen in Deutschland wird deutlich: Wir können es uns als Gesellschaft und Wirtschaftsstandort nicht leisten, auf Erfahrung, Kompetenz und Engagement von Frauen zu verzichten.

Um mehr Frauen in Beschäftigung zu bringen, braucht es die richtigen Rahmenbedingungen. Ein zentraler Hebel ist dabei mehr #Flexibilität in der Arbeitszeit. Starre Vorgaben, wann und wie gearbeitet wird, sind in Zeiten von KI und digitaler Arbeit nicht mehr zeitgemäß. Die Einführung einer Wochenarbeitszeit kann hier ein wirkungsvolles Instrument sein: Sie ermöglicht es vielen Menschen, ihre Arbeitszeit auszuweiten und gleichzeitig Beruf und Privatleben selbstbestimmter zu vereinbaren.

Als einer der größten Arbeitgeber in Deutschland schaffen wir bereits heute – im Rahmen der gesetzlichen Möglichkeiten – vielfältige Optionen, um genau das zu unterstützen.

Doch klar ist auch: Ohne mutige politische Rahmenbedingungen und ein gemeinsames Verständnis von moderner Arbeit werden wir das vorhandene Potenzial nicht heben. Wenn wir Transformation wirklich gestalten wollen, müssen wir Vielfalt konsequent fördern, Flexibilität ermöglichen und die Arbeitswelt an die Realität der Menschen anpassen.


Bundesministerium für Bildung, Familie, Senioren, Frauen und Jugend | DIW Berlin - German Institute for Economic Research

After Davos, action begins.

The conversations were valuable. Now comes the hard work of turning them into action.

In my latest article, I share a few reflections from the conversations I had with the people at Davos and what they signal for the road ahead.

I’d love to hear: what actions are you taking after #WEF26?

𝐈𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐀𝐈, 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐣𝐨𝐛, 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲?

That question framed our panel hosted by KPMG at AI House Davos during World Economic Forum. Together with May Habib and Alessandro De Luca, and moderated by Ashish Madan, we explored how AI and agentic systems are changing the very nature of work and organizations.

👉 A few reflections I keep coming back to:

1️⃣ What still defines a #job? 
A job is, fundamentally, a bundle of tasks or activities performed to achieve a certain outcome. What changes with AI is how these tasks are bundled –through automation or augmentation – and by whom they are performed: humans, machines, and agents. From an economic perspective, jobs are outcome-driven, balancing input and output. And yet, for us humans, a job is more than that. It is also about connection, identity, and purpose.

2️⃣ Transformation stands and falls with #people.
We tend to over-index on tools and technology, but 80% of change is behavioral and cultural. People’s engagement, rooted in trust and psychological safety, determines how fast organizations can really move.

3️⃣ #Leadership faces a paradox: “everything changes – and nothing changes.”
In the age of AI, it is the role of leaders to decide what business they are in and what purpose guides it. And they need to stay in control of what matters most. Leaders remain accountable for business models, quality, ethical decision-making, etc. The fundamentals – trust, empowerment, psychological safety and a growth mindset – matter just as much in the age of AI, if not more.

4️⃣ Which #organizations are we ultimately building?
AI will not lead to radical change unless we rethink our processes and operating models. The real question is which organizations we are ultimately building. This is not about incremental change, but about redesigning systems and enabling new ways of working. We need to be deliberate about where we automate tasks and where we augment human capability. And we must always keep humans in the loop – or even in the lead – because this is where human skills – such as judgment, contextual understanding, and purpose – remain essential.

I remain positive – yet not naive about AI. It can be a powerful enabler, helping us rethink industry, address demographic challenges, democratize knowledge, and protect our planet. 

In the end, the answers often do not lie in the technology alone.
They lie in the choices we make – and in how consciously and purposefully we apply technology, together.

It was a joy and a privilege to talk Circularity at the One Young World Summit in Munich, looking out to a room full of brilliant young leaders. I had the opportunity to engage on a topic that holds immense relevance for us today: how can we learn from circularity in nature and marry those eons of „R&D“ with today’s technology to get back to balance.
 
Life on this planet has always been circular. The ancient rhythm of cycles turns fallen leaves into soil, and returns a river’s water back to the sky. Everything in nature is interconnected. Every end is a new beginning.
And for the longest time, mankind lived by the rules and rhythm of nature - and its resourcefulness.

Yet with industrialization and globalization, we replaced the circle with a straight line - Take. Make. Dispose. The linear model seemed like a promise of growth and prosperity - but not for everyone, and it stretches our planet’s limits.

Now it's time to rebalance. We must decouple growth from resource consumption and change the operating model of the world from linear back to circular.

In this transformation to „circular by design“, technology is our most potent ally. AI and digital twins are enablers of breakthrough innovation in the digital world - with positive impact in the real world. 

Our wonderful young leaders and changemakers will be architects of renewal. If they - we all - choose the circle over the straight line. 

 So, let’s make the circle whole again – together!

80% of companies struggle to capture returns from their Gen AI investments, according to a 2025 McKinsey survey.

So how can we translate #GenAI potential into real #productivity?

There’s no simple answer – but #experimentation brings us closer.

The new Harvard Business Review article captures an important truth: the path to productivity isn’t linear. It’s a “J-curve” that requires a learning mindset and the courage to test, adapt, and scale what really works.

I’m pleased to see this approach, which we embrace at Siemens, featured in the article. For us, it’s experimentation that puts people at the center. In 2024, we ran the first test of our #IndustrialCopilot – a GenAI-powered shop-floor assistant – at our factory in Erlangen. Our maintenance engineers found it saved them time. But the real surprise came from our technicians – especially the more junior and less experienced staff – who said it helped them tackle complex issues more confidently, particularly on night shifts when no engineers were around.

This is what we mean by #TechnologywithPurpose: empowering people, enabling continuous learning, and ensuring digitalization delivers real value for our workforce and customers.

When used well, AI makes HR more human, not less. The move that matters is embedding it where the work already happens. As automations take on more of the complex, multi-step tasks, our people can spend more of their time on what technology cannot do: being present, building trust, and being a real human interface to the business.

That's why leadership itself sits at the centre. The job is no longer to keep things steady. It is to grow people who hold a clear direction while their surroundings shift, and to turn our executive programmes into everyday practice.

The same honesty has to apply to how we run the function. The real gain comes from doing things once and well, as one team, and that takes leaders willing to question how we work.

Why do I keep going on pilgrimage year after year?
 
People walk the Camino de Santiago for many reasons. Some are fulfilling a lifelong dream, whilst others walk for spiritual reasons, to recover from an illness or to come to terms with the loss of a loved one.

For me, it is also an endeavour where the journey is the destination. It has become a personal tradition that during springtime I walk a stretch of it. This year I covered 175 kilometres from La Romieu to Argagnon in France on the Via Podiensis. I cherish these days of being in beautiful nature all day, without meetings nor screens, when my mind can settle, and my body finds the soothing rhythm of the trail.
 
What I find there is something that everyday life rarely affords me: genuine time to reflect, to recharge my batteries and to draw strength. The daily 5 to 7-hour walks carry an element of resilience too. Everyone walks at their own pace and meets their own personal limits. Nothing else allows me to do this in quite the same way.
 
I also cherish the exchange with like-minded pilgrims from all over the world, whom you meet on the trail or over dinner in the lodgings – this year Canadians, Australians, Scots, Israelis, Swiss and Dutch. Despite our different paths and backgrounds, we share the same beautiful experience and many a good conversation.
 
I'm returning to my desk with (let's be honest) slightly tired legs but energised with a fresh and clear mind. Whilst I'm already looking forward to next year's stage over the Pyrenees, the impressions of the last few days will stay with me for quite some time. 🥾

The recipe matters more than the kitchen.
 
That is the title and the central finding of the first paper published by our RWE Commercial AI Lab in Bellevue, Washington State. It argues that in AI weather prediction, how you train a model – the data it learns from, the methods used, what it is rewarded for getting right – matters at least as much as the design of the model itself.
 
The initial findings from our AI Lab are quite something, as they offer direct business value. Better weather prediction means sharper trading decisions, smarter dispatch of renewable assets, and stronger resilience when extremes hit the grid.
 
My sincere thanks to the four authors of the paper: Piyush Garg, Diana Gergel, and Galen Yacalis from our Commercial AI Lab, as well as Andrew Shao, PhD from Hewlett Packard Enterprise. You brought the recipe to the kitchen!
 
Why this matters beyond academia:
 
▪︎ NVIDIA Earth-2 Open Models (FCN3, Atlas) and ECMWF’s AIFS-Ens ranked higher than other models in the overall model assessment. However, no single model performed consistently across all the metrics, thus suggesting that the choice of training pipeline matters more than choosing the right architecture.
▪︎ The study's impact is already resonating within academic institutions and wider groups working on building AI weather models. NVIDIA teams have reached out directly.
▪︎ Using NVIDIA Earth2Studio – the open framework now standard for testing AI weather models – the team validated the results across ten architectures, thirty initialisation dates and four extreme events – the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome, the Texas freeze, Winter Storm Elliott and the 2023 heatwave in Europe.
 
What I find most compelling is how this work positions RWE and our research team at the AI Lab as a contributor to the science the AI field depends on. The energy transition runs on forecasts and some of the science behind them is now being shaped at RWE.

AI for value. Humans at the centre. Real impact only happens when AI is truly embedded into everyday work – not as a concept, but as part of how decisions are made, processes run, and teams collaborate.
 
Last week at the Government Innovation Board hosted by GovTech Deutschland, I shared how we at RWE are working with AI, particularly in the context of agentic AI.
 
Four key messages shaped my speech:
 
▪︎ The division of labour is shifting, but the human stays at the centre: Agentic systems prepare tasks, weigh up options and flag where action is needed – always within clear guardrails. Speed, structuring and pattern recognition move to the system. Judgement and decision-making authority remain with people.
▪︎ Real innovation happens in concrete workflows – where processes are genuinely understood and responsibility is lived.
▪︎ Governance builds trust and resilience: AI governance is not optional – it is the foundation for safe, transparent and responsible AI use at scale.
▪︎ AI challenges leadership: leaders must become role models in learning and using AI. Change management is crucial for a successful AI transformation.
 
One thing became clear once again: public administration and industry are working towards a shared agenda – building capabilities, strengthening trust, and scaling AI responsibly – even if at different stages.
 
Many thanks to Markus Richter and Achim Berg for the invitation and dialogue, and to Bernd Gemein for sharing the Deutsche Post perspective.

Leadership has never been about certainty; it has much rather been about helping others move forward without it.
 
End of last week, over 170 colleagues from near and far gathered in Copenhagen for our 7th RWE Group Leadership Meeting. What made this year’s meeting truly special to me was the collective energy in the room which was filled with a sense of purpose, determination and vision. 
 
This year’s theme: Living Leadership. This was chosen because we’re currently witnessing three profound shifts happening simultaneously:

▪︎ Speed and complexity: We are scaling our portfolio, our partnerships and our geographies at pace. Decisions must be driven by competitive outcomes, not by waiting for perfect information, which in the current environment is rarely available.
▪︎ Technology and AI: AI is transforming the tools available to us, creating new opportunities but also uncertainties around accountability, skills, and where human judgement ends and the algorithm begins. AI is not an IT initiative. It is a leadership topic that is relevant to every one of us.
▪︎ Permanent transformation: Change is no longer a phase. It is the operating condition. In this world, resilience is not a soft skill; it is an organisational capability. And the instinct to control complexity can become a liability. Leadership is about creating clarity and adaptability under pressure.

In practice, Living Leadership comes down to the following factors: being explicit about priorities and trade-offs; owning decisions even when AI has shaped the analysis; building teams that are empowered enough to act and where it is safe enough to speak up. But it is also our personal responsibility – leading others requires a strong self. We as leaders need to be fit for future, confident, curious, and capable of performing in this uncompromised environment.  

That is how resilience is built – not through comfort, but through capability.
 
Thank you to everyone involved for two days of clear thinking and meaningful conversations.

Industrial history and personal history are rarely far apart. That connection became very real when 91-year-old Paul Diestelhorst opened his photo albums and gave us a glimpse into a life shaped by the power station in Frimmersdorf. A rare and valuable insight.
 
The demolition of cooling tower Q at the end of February made the connection very tangible. The enormous steel and concrete chimney was built in the 1960s as part of what would become Europe's largest power station at that time. It is a significant part of our company's history and of the region's industrial identity.
 
At the age of 19, Paul came to Frimmersdorf in search of work. What followed was an entire working life with RWE – from power plant operator to control room operator to foreman. He knew every corner of tower Q. And at this advanced age, he witnessed the demolition of the very structure that he helped build and operate for decades.
 
Stories like Paul’s demonstrate to me what makes RWE stand out as an employer: the recognition of every single employee’s contribution. Day in, day out, shift after shift, on land and at sea.
 
With RWE’s accelerated phase-out of coal by 2030, a chapter of industrial history is coming to an end. And at the same time, our story continues. The Frimmersdorf site, for example, will be transformed into an innovative digital and transformation hub, and key parts of the power station will be preserved in the spirit of industrial heritage conservation. That is what RWE stands for: knowing and respecting our history yet always looking ahead and shaping the future.
 
Thank you, Paul, for everything you have achieved and given to #TeamRWE.

Cybersecurity is a top priority for RWE. After all, cyberattacks on critical infrastructure are no longer the exception – they are part of our everyday reality.

Yesterday, I spoke about precisely this topic at the Digitalk meets ZACTALK event (Digitale Stadt Düsseldorf e.V.) at XPONENTIAL Europe and highlighted three key perspectives:

▪︎ Cybersecurity is a key factor in building trust: for our employees, for our partners and for society, which relies on a reliable energy supply at all times.
▪︎ Cybersecurity as a strategic issue: cybersecurity is managed just like any other key management and risk issue: transparently, taking a risk-aware approach and an integrated view of resilience.
▪︎ The corporate culture dimension: sustainable cybersecurity is effective not only in systems, but also in day-to-day actions and through mindset. It requires informed, attentive, and empowered employees and managers who actively exemplify security. At RWE, we bring this to life through a variety of formats – from web-based trainings and phishing simulations to live hacking sessions and escape rooms.

AI is a particular focus. It is fundamentally changing the risk landscape, including in the field of cybercrime. Precisely because AI-powered cyberattacks specifically target the human factor, human judgement becomes more important – not less so.

For RWE, this means that cybersecurity does not end with prevention. Strong detection and response capabilities, clear responsibilities and a security culture that is put into practice form the foundation for a secure energy transition without disruption.

It is not every day that industry, law enforcement and the military sit down together to discuss security and economic policy perspectives. Thank you for this enriching discussion Manfred Boudreaux-Dehmer, Markus Hartmann, Jens Elstermeier and Stephan Schneider for chairing.

Warum will niemand mehr Führungskraft werden?

Das wollte DER SPIEGEL von Heike Bruch wissen. Sie ist die Herausgeberin der St. Galler Jugendstudie, die drei Kipppunkte ausgemacht hat, wieso junge Menschen keine Lust mehr auf Führungspositionen haben.

Vorgesetzte wirken oft ausgebrannt und in einer Arbeitsmühle, die wenig erfüllend wirkt. Junge Menschen nehmen Strukturen als alt und starr wahr. Und: Führungskräfte spüren oft eine Überforderung oder das Gefühl, am Limit zu arbeiten, sodass sie ihre Führungsaufgaben am liebsten wieder abgeben möchten.

Die Quintessenz – und auch mein Erleben aus meinem beruflichen Alltag: Es fehlt dem Nachwuchs nicht an Ehrgeiz, sondern mitunter an Möglichkeiten, Verantwortung zu erproben, und auch an Vorbildern, die zeigen: So sieht gute Führung aus. So macht Führung Spaß.

Wir bei RWE sind uns unserer Verantwortung, Führungskräfte kontinuierlich auszubilden, bewusst. Zunächst einmal ist es sicherlich erfreulich, dass wir bei RWE keinen Mangel an Mitarbeitenden haben, die Führungsaufgaben übernehmen möchten. Nun liegt es an uns, eine Umgebung zu schaffen, die sich von der oben skizzierten deutlich unterscheidet. Dazu zählt, dass wir unsere Führungskräfte und Potenzialträger auf ihrer Reise begleiten und unterstützen.

Für den Gesamtkonzern haben wir unser Führungskräfteprogramm, unsere RWE Executive Journey, weiter geschärft. In Linie mit unserem Purpose, unseren Unternehmenswerten und unseren erfolgskritischen Verhaltensweisen haben wir ein gemeinsames Führungsverständnis definiert: Unsere RWE Leadership Principles. Diese Führungsprinzipien folgen klaren Standards und formulieren eine klare Erwartung, wie gute Führung bei RWE gelebt wird:

▪︎ Lead for Business Impact
▪︎ Lead to Deliver
▪︎ Lead for Team Success

Eine Umgebung zu schaffen, in der unsere Mitarbeitenden am besten wachsen und wirken können, liegt an uns. Wir begleiten unsere Führungskräfte auf jedem Schritt ihrer Reise und bereiten sie strukturiert auf ihre Rolle vor. Das gilt für das gesamte Spektrum von der ersten Führungsrolle, der Weiterentwicklung als Führungskraft oder einem Neueinstieg bis zum Gesellschaftswechsel.

Wichtig ist uns auch: Leadership ist nicht immer eine lineare Entwicklung, sondern hochindividuell: Es gibt auch Möglichkeiten zurück in Fachpositionen, geteilte Führungsrollen oder Sabbaticals als Möglichkeiten, neue Perspektiven kennenzulernen.

Unsere RWE Executive Journey unterstützt kontinuierlich, leitet an und ermutigt, den Schritt in die Führungsverantwortung zu gehen. Ein großer Dank an die vielen HR Kolleginnen und Kollegen aus dem gesamten Konzern, die gemeinsam RWEs Weg an dieser Stelle unterstützen.

Ich bin schon sehr gespannt, wie sich die Ergebnisse in unserem Unternehmen widerspiegeln werden. Denn ich bin überzeugt: Führung ist attraktiv!

Bleiben wir Anwender oder ist unser Anspruch bei KI ein anderer?
 
Unter anderem darum ging es bei „Allianz der Chancen trifft… Lars Klingbeil“ gestern in Berlin. Die Arbeitswelt geht in die nächste Phase über. Und die gelingt nur im Zusammenspiel zwischen echter und künstlicher Intelligenz. 
 
Im Fokus der Gespräche stand daher, wie eng Finanzpolitik, technologische Entwicklung und Beschäftigung miteinander verbunden sind. Investitionen in Infrastruktur – wie zuletzt in die KI-Fabrik in München – sind zweifelsohne eine wichtige Grundlage. Entscheidend ist jedoch, ob wir Anwender bleiben oder den Anspruch entwickeln, Weltmarktführer für KI-gestützte Geschäftsmodelle zu werden – und ob wir KI dabei konsequent menschenzentriert denken. 
 
Dafür braucht es die Mitarbeitenden aller Unternehmen, die sich in der Allianz der Chancen zusammengeschlossen haben. KI und Mensch müssen dabei Hand in Hand gehen. Auch in dem Bewusstsein, die richtige Tonalität zu treffen, um auf die Ängste vieler Menschen zu reagieren. Mein Eindruck ist, dass wir uns bei Unsicherheit oftmals wieder an alten Verhaltensmustern bedienen, die wir eigentlich schon geglaubt, überwunden zu haben. Hier wünsche ich mir ein gemeinsames Narrativ, eine gemeinsame Strategie aus Politik und Wirtschaft. 
  
Ein herzliches Dankeschön an Ulrike Zeiler für die Gastfreundschaft im Allianz-Forum, an Vizekanzler und Bundesminister Lars Klingbeil für den Impuls, an Dr. Ariane Reinhart für die Moderation und an alle Teilnehmenden für den offenen Austausch und die inspirierenden Perspektiven. So leisten Formate wie die Allianz der Chancen einen wichtigen Beitrag für die Arbeitswelt von morgen.

The way AI is shaped will shape the world!
 
The question therefore is: Do we want to remove biases or reinforce blind spots? One alarm signal for the latter is that various studies indicate only around 22-30% of global AI talent is female.
 
At RWE, however, we strive to do the former. We want AI in our organisation to reflect the perspectives, creativity, and empathy of everyone – not just a few. This week I had the pleasure of joining the launch event for our Women in AI network. The network brings together women from different functions across teams and countries, creating a space to connect, learn, and experiment. It’s about more than representation – it’s about enabling women to actively and responsibly shape AI in ethical, inclusive ways.
 
During the discussion I shared my view of AI as a key enabler of digital transformation and the energy transition. And about what is needed in terms of a strong foundation for AI to scale. It's what I call a golden triangle consisting of:
▪️HR – to bring purpose and heart
▪️IT – to drive innovation
▪️Security – to provide the trust that allows us to move fast without breaking things
 
Together, they form the foundation of an organisation where AI can act as a co-pilot, supporting employees and freeing up time for creative, strategic work by humans. This is where women make a real difference. Women often bring strong domain expertise, ethical awareness, and empathy. Diverse teams reduce blind spots and help build robust AI solutions that are fairer and more sustainable. 
 
This was a successful start to the network, and I am already very excited to see the first tangible results. Thanks to Thomas Denny and Marina Sverdel for the lively discussion on stage and huge congratulations to Gülnaz Öneş and the women on the AI core team for making this network possible.

“Turning points”
“Geopolitical storms”
Uncertainty is no longer the exception, it’s now part of leadership.
 
How do uncertainty and a rapidly changing world shape the way we lead? This was a topic in the panel discussion with Colette Rückert-Hennen we had at  The London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) German Symposium.
 
From my personal perspective – being responsible for HR, IT and Security – the challenge is even more fundamental: We are moving from an era of efficiency to an era of agency. The past decades, leadership was about managing “Human Resources”. Now, AI is finally taking the 'robot' out of the job. It is absorbing the management chores, the data-drudgery, and the administrative friction. This creates spaces. New possibilities. 

The big question for us on this panel is: What would be the wisest way to fill the newly created spaces? Our shared conviction: If we manage to fill it with Human Agency - transparency, radical vulnerability, and shared leadership - we turn uncertainty into our greatest competitive advantage. My goal is to use technology as a multiplier, not a replacer, so that our collective time becomes our company’s most valuable asset.

Are women better prepared for uncertain times, as there is something called the "female" leadership style? 

I try to avoid stereotypes, but research shows that in times of high stress, there is the temptation to revert to autocratic styles when the world feels 'Brittle' or 'Incomprehensible' (BANI). It feels safe to have one person 'set the course.' But I have to argue the opposite. Autocracy is a bottleneck. In an era where AI agents are processing data and making micro-decisions in milliseconds, an autocratic leader becomes the slowest part of the system. An autocratic leader who pretends to have all the answers creates a fragile organisation. A leader who shows vulnerability and transparency creates a resilient one. In a BANI world, collaboration is a survival skill, not a 'soft' skill. And so is Diversity!

My first business trip this year, and I'm returning with a lot of insights and impressions.

The last days in Vietnam were dense and fully packed. Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City: Two site visits with our partner FPT Software, where parts of our IT services are delivered and where we are currently further exploring our Best Shoring Model. Every conversation focused on capability, reliability, and long-term performance rather than short-term optimisation. 

The same mindset was apparent at FPT University. A very holistic view on education: Computer science is central, of course, but every student is required to also study English, practises Vietnamese martial arts, and learns to play a traditional musical instrument. Performance, they showed me, grows not from technical skills alone, but from discipline, balance, and cultural grounding. That combination is remarkable. 

This perspective carried into a panel on Women in Tech and Energy, which I opened with a speech while wearing a beautiful traditional Vietnamese dress. We spoke about technology, but the deeper question was how to prepare people for what comes next. At RWE, a human-first approach means using AI to support people: to simplify work, increase efficiency, and create space for strategic thinking, creativity, and developing new capabilities.

I see women playing a dedicated role in the AI transformation. We must lean in when AI models and LLMs are trained, ensuring that the future AI world is at least as diverse as today's. And this commitment comes to life in the field, as we noticed during our visits to Offshore Delivery Centres and the AI Campus in Saigon, where we saw AI already processing vast data sets in real time and accelerating development cycles from months to days, all underpinned by a performance culture built on clarity, ownership, and ambition. 

I leave Vietnam with gratitude for the openness and generosity of everyone who shared their insights – especially Chu Thi Thanh Ha and all colleagues at FPT Software. 

Happy Lunar New Year next month to everyone celebrating.

Let's start the year with a view!
 
After taking you on a virtual tour of a wind turbine, today we're heading to the “heart” of the offshore wind farm: the substation.
 
What you see here is the offshore substation of our Kaskasi wind farm, 35 km off the coast of Heligoland. The substation is the central hub where electricity from all turbines comes together before heading to shore. From the outside, it might seem like just another platform at sea, but inside it’s a giant tangle of components and connections, all designed to make the flow of electricity reliable and continuous.
 
What kind of work goes into this heart of an offshore wind farm? Nothing less than an engineering masterpiece in manufacturing, heavy-lift vessels to transport the thousands of tonnes of topside components, and absolute precision during the “marriage” at sea – the installation of the topside onto the foundation. 
 
Once completed, the wind turbines turn, the generators produce electricity, and this is fed into the relevant grid connections via the substation. Sounds simple – but take a look for yourself! It’s easy to forget, from the outside, just how much care and coordination goes into making everything work. 
 
Looking ahead, RWE Offshore Wind will deliver four construction projects with a total capacity of 4.8 GW and continue providing clean, reliable electricity from our wind farms. Considering the dedication that goes into every detail, it’s clear that none of this would be possible without #TeamRWE.

AI transformation is a journey. That's true for us at RWE, too. 
 
For me, the goal of the journey is clear: We want to become a best-in-class company that seamlessly integrates human expertise with agentic capabilities! The areas of application are diverse, ranging for example from process improvements to site layouts for offshore wind farms or weather models for our trading business.
 
What vehicles are we using to embark on this journey? A very important one is the Promptathon. It brings users and technology together, in a kind of laboratory environment where employees can bring specific concerns and then experiment with them. The impact is proven: we know from past projects that we can go from an idea to a prototype within a day. I find that remarkable and I am confident and excited about the future.
 
Many thanks to Dr. Max Schumm and Scott-Oliver Luehrs for your commitment in preparing and running the Promptathons and for the insights into the status quo of our journey.

My personal AI vision for RWE: We will become a best-in-class company that seamlessly integrates human expertise with agentic capabilities!
 
After a week on the US west coast, one thing is clear: AI is everywhere. From the Microsoft Ignite Conference to our very own AI Lab in Seattle – it was the predominant subject. Together with our CIO Gülnaz Öneş, the first item on the agenda was the Microsoft Ignite Conference in San Francisco. My highlights:

•   A use case for AI in the energy sector
•   Playbooks from manufacturing companies
•   Future possibilities of agents and targeted hands-on prompting
 
The inspiration continued at RWE's own Commercial AI Research Lab. Founded in mid-2023, around 15 employees are now working intensively on probabilistic AI weather forecasts, scientific research into weather and climate, and commercial weather models. They are working on coding complex and chaotic interactions across multiple domains to maximise the value of weather data. What else remains from a week full of AI? Personal, human interaction remains the most enjoyable aspect, whether in the office or with family and friends. With this in mind, I would like to wish all our American colleagues a Happy Thanksgiving.

Leadership is changing. And it makes me genuinely proud to see how these shifts are taking shape within RWE.
 
Last week I met Melanie Peter and Claudia Neumann, two colleagues who share one role as Head of Corporate Finance EU & APAC. What they have created goes far beyond dividing tasks. It shows what shared responsibility can mean when it becomes a real form of leadership.
 
The idea of job sharing grew over time – from a conversation about flexibility and new ways of leading. Both worked part-time, both were ambitious, and both realised how well their strengths complemented each other. What began as a simple thought became a shared leadership model they shaped with intention.
 
Job sharing gives two leaders the space to combine responsibility with balance. It allows them to bring different perspectives to one role and gives their teams continuity and clarity. For us as an organisation, it helps people stay on a leadership path during different phases of their lives and strengthens how we work together overall. 
 
When I spoke with Melanie and Claudia, I was struck by how clearly they structure their work. They have defined who leads on which topics, they keep each other informed on the issues that matter most and they step in for one another without hesitation. Strategic decisions and key people topics are made together, which gives their teams consistency and a clear direction. Their partnership is focused, confident and deeply human, and it shows how shared leadership can be both decisive and balanced.
 
Now, after a year in their shared role, their conclusion is clear: it works. It delivers. And it keeps evolving. This is not an experiment. It is progress in motion.
 
For me, their story captures what leadership at #TeamRWE is about: trust, curiosity, and the courage to rethink what is possible together. Because transformation is not a strategy on paper. It starts with people who lead differently – and it ends with a company that grows stronger because of it.

Ready for new perspectives? Step inside an offshore wind turbine — at least virtually 😉.
 
Offshore wind is one of our key technologies in generating low-carbon electricity. Close to 200 metres above sea level is where ambition meets teamwork. #TeamRWE currently has around 5 GW of installed capacity of offshore wind under construction — in parallel, across three countries! Earlier this week, we celebrated milestones that three out of four construction projects finalised foundation installation and are ready (or already in full swing) for turbine installation.
 
Reason enough to share with you a glimpse of what it looks like in one of our powerful 9-MW turbines at our offshore wind farm Kaskasi, which is located 35km off the coast of Heligoland: 81-metre blades, a rotor span roughly the size of three football fields. Pure engineering brilliance. But take a look for yourself and enjoy the insights from boat landing up to the nacelle!
 
And while new turbines keep rising, our Operations and Maintenance teams make sure everything runs smoothly across a growing number of wind farms and turbines. Their work keeps this progress alive — steady, reliable, and safe. I am grateful for everyone who makes that possible every single day.

We are transforming our core business. Major investments, new technologies, innovative ideas – these are obvious and visible. But our technological transformation to a low-carbon business model is only one dimension. 
 
A recent study by Fraunhofer HNFIZ demonstrates the complexity of transformation. It explored what factors enable companies to manage transformation successfully. Using AI, the researchers analysed more than 250,000 scientific publications and identified 31 key factors grouped into five dimensions: 
 
• Leadership and governance 
• Culture and collaboration 
• Resources and intellectual property 
• Technology and data 
• Ecosystems and markets 
 
The message is clear: technology is only one part of the picture. Human connection, learning and trust turn transformation into lasting progress. 
 
At RWE, this is our daily reality. The energy transition reaches every corner of the company — technical, organisational and cultural. Every day, #TeamRWE is adapting - taking on new responsibilities, sharing knowledge in new ways, and finding practical ways to support one another through constant change. 
 
As leaders, it is our responsibility to create the right environment for this to happen, spaces for learning, opportunities for open dialogue and building the confidence that everyone can help shape this journey. Because transformation doesn’t happen to people; a joint commitment turns change into lasting success.

Turning safety into something you can experience – that’s the idea behind our new Safety Tour at the RWE Campus in Essen.
 
Health and safety is our number one priority at our power plant sites and in our offices. We have created an interactive guided tour with seven stations across the campus. Topics include ergonomics, occupational health care, emergency management, fire extinguishers and first aid, escape routes and assembly points, business travel, and walking safely on campus. Each stop turns theory into practice with clear information and practical tasks. This hands-on format brings theory to life and fosters active dialogue in an engaging manner, as managers and employees work their way through the tour together.
 
I really like our new safety tour because it’s a smart way making health and safety tangible and part of our everyday work - not just a checklist!
 
Many thanks to Kay Paßlack, Heike Bruckmann and Frank Topp for developing and implementing this inspiring format.
